qs.q: Which of the following are correct preparation steps before an abdominal assessment?
c: Good lighting
Have client empty bladder
Supine with arms at sides or across chest and knees bent or on pillow
Warm hands & stethoscope; short fingernails
Ask client to cough forcefully while you palpate
qs.e: Good lighting, an empty bladder, proper positioning/draping, warm hands, and asking about tenderness improve client comfort and accuracy of the exam.

qs.q: When inspecting abdominal contour, the profile is determined from the rib margin to the:
c: Pubic bone
Umbilicus
Xiphoid process
Anterior superior iliac spine
qs.e: Contour is judged by the profile traced from the rib margin down to the pubic bone.

qs.q: Abdominal contour describes the client's:
c: Nutritional state
Kidney function
Bowel motility
Sensory status
qs.e: Contour reflects nutritional status and normally ranges from flat to rounded.

qs.q: The abdominal contour normally ranges from ______ to rounded.
c: flat
qs.e: Normal contour runs from flat to rounded; the slides list no other normal extremes.

qs.q: During abdominal inspection, asking the client to take a deep breath may help make which of these more visible?
c: Masses and enlarged organs
Bowel sounds
Rebound tenderness
Referred pain
qs.e: Deep inspiration can lift organs and masses under the rib margin so localized bulging becomes easier to see.

qs.q: A normal umbilicus is:
c: Midline and inverted
Midline and everted
Right of midline and discolored
Left of midline and raised
qs.e: The umbilicus should sit midline and be inverted, with no discoloration, inflammation, or hernia.

qs.q: Which findings are normal on umbilical inspection?
c: Midline and inverted
No sign of discoloration
No sign of inflammation
No sign of hernia
Protruding and erythematous
qs.e: All four are normal; a protruding or discolored umbilicus would be abnormal.

qs.q: A fine venous network may be visible on the abdominal skin of:
c: Thin persons
Obese persons
Dehydrated clients
Clients with ascites
qs.e: In thin clients the superficial venous network can show through the skin and is a normal finding.

qs.q: One common pigment change to note on the abdomen is:
c: Striae
Petechiae
Kernicterus
Tinel sign
qs.e: Striae (stretch marks) are a common pigment change on the abdomen and are routinely noted.

qs.q: If a surgical scar is present on the abdomen, the nurse should assess its cause and document:
c: Location and length
Width and color
Shape and height
Texture only
qs.e: The slides direct the nurse to assess the cause of the scar and document its location and length.

qs.q: Pigmented nevi on the abdomen are described as:
c: Circumscribed brown macular or papular areas
Yellow raised cysts
Red raised pustules
Round fluid-filled blisters
qs.e: Pigmented nevi (moles) are common on the abdomen and appear as circumscribed brown macular or papular areas.

qs.q: A visible aortic pulsation beneath the skin is normally seen in which area, especially in thin persons?
c: Epigastric
Hypogastric
Left lower quadrant
Umbilical
qs.e: Aortic pulsations can normally be seen in the epigastric area, especially in thin clients with relaxed muscle walls.

qs.q: Respiratory movement shows in the abdomen particularly in:
c: Males
Females
Neonates
Obese clients
qs.e: The slides note respiratory movement is most visible abdominally in males.

qs.q: Waves of peristalsis are sometimes visible in very ______ persons.
c: thin
qs.e: Visible peristalsis is a normal finding limited to very thin clients with thin abdominal walls.

qs.q: Bowel sound auscultation should begin in the:
c: Right lower quadrant
Left lower quadrant
Right upper quadrant
Umbilical area
qs.e: Bowel sounds are assessed for character and frequency beginning in the RLQ.

qs.q: Which part of the stethoscope is used to auscultate bowel sounds?
c: Diaphragm
Bell
Both bell and diaphragm
Neither; use direct auscultation
qs.e: The diaphragm is used to auscultate bowel sounds.

qs.q: Normal bowel sounds are described as:
c: High pitched, gurgling, cascading
Low pitched, rumbling, distant
Rushing, tinkling, loud
Silent with no audible sounds
qs.e: Normal bowel sounds are high pitched, gurgling, and cascading in nature.

qs.q: Hyperactive bowel sounds are caused primarily by:
c: Increased motility
Decreased motility
Peritoneal irritation
Absent peristalsis
qs.e: Hyperactive sounds (loud, high pitched, rushing, tinkling) reflect increased intestinal motility.

qs.q: Which conditions are associated with hyperactive bowel sounds?
c: Early obstruction
Gastroenteritis
Laxatives
Subsiding paralytic ileus
Peritonitis
qs.e: All four are linked to increased motility; peritonitis is instead associated with hypoactive or absent bowel sounds.

qs.q: Which conditions are associated with hypoactive or absent bowel sounds?
c: Abdominal surgery
Peritonitis
Paralytic ileus
Complete obstruction
Gastroenteritis
qs.e: All four suppress bowel sounds; gastroenteritis produces hyperactive sounds instead.

qs.q: Before declaring bowel sounds absent, how long must the nurse auscultate continuously?
c: 5 minutes
2 minutes
1 minute
10 minutes
qs.e: ⚠ Conflict: Slide 17 (her method) requires continuous auscultation of all 4 quadrants starting RLQ for 5 minutes before declaring bowel sounds absent; Jarvis states that auscultating all 4 quadrants is not necessary.

qs.q: Vascular sounds or bruits should be auscultated over which of these arteries?
c: Abdominal aorta
Renal arteries
Iliac arteries
Femoral arteries
Carotid arteries
qs.e: The four abdominal/pelvic vessels listed are auscultated for bruits; carotids are not part of this exam.

qs.q: Percussion of the abdomen is used primarily to:
c: Assess relative density of abdominal contents
Determine liver span
Test deep tendon reflexes
Assess muscle strength
qs.e: Percussion assesses relative density, locates organs, and screens for abnormal fluid or masses — but Slide 21 states it is not recommended for liver span.

qs.q: Tympany is described as:
c: High pitched and musical
Medium intensity, duration and pitch
Very loud intensity with low pitch
Absent sound
qs.e: Tympany is a high-pitched, musical sound produced by air in the stomach and intestines.

qs.q: Presence of air in the stomach and intestines produces which percussion sound?
c: Tympany
Dullness
Hyperresonance
Flatness
qs.e: Tympany is the normal percussion note over gas-filled bowel and stomach.

qs.q: Dullness is described as:
c: Medium intensity, duration and pitch
High pitched and musical
Very loud intensity, low pitch, long duration
Silent with no tone
qs.e: Dullness is a medium-intensity, medium-duration, medium-pitch sound.

qs.q: Dullness on abdominal percussion may indicate presence of:
c: Solid organs
Masses
Fluid
Distended bladder
Gaseous distention
qs.e: All four cause dullness; gaseous distention produces hyperresonance instead.

qs.q: Hyperresonance is described as:
c: Very loud intensity, low pitch, long duration
High pitched and musical
Medium intensity and pitch
Absent tone
qs.e: Hyperresonance is very loud, low-pitched, and long in duration; it signals gaseous distention.

qs.q: Hyperresonance on abdominal percussion is associated with:
c: Gaseous distention
Solid organ enlargement
Fluid accumulation
Fat deposition
qs.e: Hyperresonance reflects trapped gas causing gaseous distention of the bowel.

qs.q: Percussion is NOT recommended for determining:
c: Liver span
Splenomegaly
Bladder distention
Kidney tenderness
Presence of air in the stomach
qs.e: Slide 21 lists liver span, splenomegaly, and bladder distention as inappropriate uses; CVA percussion IS used for kidney tenderness and tympany DOES indicate air.

qs.q: Percussion of the costovertebral angle is performed to assess for:
c: Kidney tenderness
Liver span
Spleen size
Bowel sounds
qs.e: CVA percussion is used specifically to elicit kidney tenderness.

qs.q: Abdominal palpation is performed to assess size, location, and consistency of certain organs and to screen for:
c: Abnormal mass or tenderness
Liver span
Bowel sounds
Kidney size
qs.e: Palpation screens for abnormal mass or tenderness in addition to organ characteristics.

qs.q: During abdominal palpation, tender areas should be assessed:
c: Last
First
Only if the client agrees
Never
qs.e: Tender areas are palpated last so guarding does not interfere with the rest of the exam.

qs.q: During palpation, the nurse should also observe the client for:
c: Non-verbal cues of discomfort
Blood pressure changes
Pupil dilation
Aphasia
qs.e: Non-verbal cues of discomfort are often the only sign of tenderness in a client who does not report pain.

qs.q: Light palpation depresses the abdominal wall approximately ______ cm.
qs.e: Light palpation uses about 1 cm of depression to assess the skin surface and superficial musculature.

qs.q: The objective of light palpation is to:
c: Form an overall impression of skin surface and superficial musculature
Search specifically for individual organs
Delineate deep masses
Detect rebound tenderness
qs.e: Light palpation is not meant to search for organs — it forms an overall impression of the surface and superficial musculature, noting resistance, guarding, and tenderness.

qs.q: Deep palpation depresses the abdominal wall approximately ______ cm.
qs.e: Deep palpation uses 5–8 cm of depression to reach intra-abdominal organs and masses.

qs.q: A bimanual technique during deep palpation is used for the:
c: Very large or obese patient
Thin patient
Infant
Patient with a hernia
qs.e: The bimanual technique helps reach deep structures in very large or obese patients.

qs.q: During deep palpation, note which characteristics of any palpable organs or masses?
c: Location
Size
Consistency
Mobility
Pigmentation
qs.e: Location, size, consistency, and mobility are the four parameters listed for palpable structures.

qs.q: Rebound tenderness is used to determine the presence of:
c: Peritoneal irritation or inflammation
Bowel obstruction
Kidney stones
Muscle strain
qs.e: Rebound tenderness is a classic test for peritoneal irritation or inflammation.

qs.q: For rebound tenderness, slowly and deeply press into the abdomen at a ______-degree angle at a non-tender area.
qs.e: The fingers press at 90 degrees to the abdomen and are then quickly withdrawn; normally no pain occurs.

qs.q: Which abnormal findings are listed in the slides for abdominal assessment?
c: Abdominal distention
Hernia
Abnormal bowel sounds
Enlarged organs
Cyanosis
qs.e: The five abnormal findings listed are abdominal distention, abdominal pain, hernia, abnormal bowel sounds, and enlarged organs; cyanosis is not in the list.

qs.q: The musculoskeletal assessment includes a functional assessment of:
c: Activities of daily living (ADLs)
Cognitive function
Visual acuity
Gustatory function
qs.e: Functional assessment of ADLs is explicitly listed as part of the musculoskeletal exam.

qs.q: Fibrous joints are:
c: Bones united by interjacent fibrous tissue or cartilage and do not move
Separated by fibrous cartilage and slightly moveable
Freely moveable joints enclosed in a synovial cavity
Hinge joints with a meniscus
qs.e: Fibrous joints are immobile; the sutures of the skull are the classic example.

qs.q: Which is an example of a fibrous joint?
c: Sutures in skull
Vertebrae
Shoulder
Knee
qs.e: Skull sutures are immovable fibrous joints; vertebrae are cartilaginous and shoulder/knee are synovial.

qs.q: Cartilaginous joints are:
c: Separated by fibrous cartilage and slightly moveable
Immovable and united by fibrous tissue
Freely moveable with a synovial membrane
Hinge-shaped and freely moveable
qs.e: Cartilaginous joints allow slight movement; the vertebrae are the example given.

qs.q: Which is an example of a cartilaginous joint?
c: Vertebrae
Sutures of skull
Shoulder
Hip
qs.e: The vertebrae are slightly moveable cartilaginous joints; the other options are fibrous or synovial.

qs.q: Synovial joints are characterized by being:
c: Freely moveable joints enclosed in a cavity lined with synovial membrane that secretes fluid
Immovable and joined by fibrous tissue
Slightly moveable with fibrous cartilage
Enclosed in a bony fusion
qs.e: Synovial joints are freely moveable; the synovial membrane lining the cavity secretes synovial fluid.

qs.q: When palpating each joint, assess for:
c: Skin temperature
Muscles
Bony articulations
Joint capsule
Pupil reaction
qs.e: Skin temperature, muscles, bony articulations, and the joint capsule are the four palpable structures listed.

qs.q: Joints are normally ______ when palpated:
c: Non-tender
Tender
Warm
Swollen
qs.e: Normal joints are non-tender; warmth and swelling are abnormal findings on inspection/palpation.

qs.q: If limitation is found during active range of motion, the nurse should next:
c: Move the joint through passive range of motion
Stop the exam
Apply ice immediately
Refer to physical therapy
qs.e: Active ROM is tested first; passive ROM follows if the client cannot complete the movement actively.

qs.q: Which findings are normally NOT present during a range of motion exam?
c: Tenderness
Pain
Crepitation
Flexion
Movement of the joint
qs.e: Tenderness, pain, and crepitation are abnormal; flexion and joint movement are normal components of ROM.

qs.q: Moving a limb away from the midline of the body is called ______.
c: abduction
qs.e: Abduction moves the limb away from the midline; adduction moves it toward the midline.

qs.q: Turning the forearm so that the palm is down is called ______.
c: pronation
qs.e: Pronation turns the palm down; supination turns the palm up.

qs.q: Moving the sole of the foot inward at the ankle is called ______.
c: inversion
qs.e: Inversion turns the sole inward; eversion turns it outward.

qs.q: Bending the limb at a joint is called ______.
c: flexion
qs.e: Flexion bends the limb at the joint; extension straightens it.

qs.q: How many grades are used when assessing muscle strength?
c: Six grades (0-5)
Five grades (1-5)
Four grades (0-3)
Ten grades (0-10)
qs.e: ⚠ Conflict: Her documentation sheet and Jarvis grade muscle strength 0–5 (six grades), while Slide 37 refers to it as a "5-point scale." Use 0–5 (six grades).

qs.q: Which instrument is used to measure joint angle during range of motion?
c: Goniometer
Sphygmomanometer
Otoscope
Tuning fork
qs.e: A goniometer is used to quantify joint angle; it is referenced at Slide 34.

qs.q: Which sequence correctly describes the abdominal assessment order emphasized in this module?
c: Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation
Auscultation, inspection, percussion, palpation
Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation
Inspection, percussion, auscultation, palpation
qs.e: Her objectives and slides state the abdomen is assessed in the order inspection, auscultation, percussion, then palpation; this is the order used on the exam. ⚠ Conflict: [Jarvis p. 545] notes that early research suggests auscultating first may not be essential, but her order [Slide 6; Slide 17] governs the exam.

qs.q: Which description matches NORMAL bowel sounds?
c: High-pitched, gurgling, and cascading
Loud, high-pitched, rushing, and tinkling
Low-pitched, rumbling, and continuous
Silent unless the client has just eaten
qs.e: Normal bowel sounds are high-pitched, gurgling, and cascading. These are the descriptors to chart under Present on the documentation sheet.

qs.q: Bowel sounds described as loud, high-pitched, rushing, and tinkling are documented as:
c: Hyperactive
Hypoactive
Absent
Within normal defined limits
qs.e: Loud, high-pitched, rushing, tinkling sounds indicate increased motility and are documented as Hyperactive on the documentation sheet.

qs.q: Which palpation technique is used for an obese client or a client with a large abdomen?
c: Bimanual palpation
Light palpation
Percussion
Rebound tenderness testing
qs.e: Deep palpation is performed with two hands (bimanual) to assess a large or obese abdomen. Note the location, size, consistency, mobility, enlargement, tenderness, and masses.

qs.q: Which maneuver correctly describes the rebound tenderness test?
c: Press slowly and deeply at 90 degrees in a non-tender area, then withdraw the hand quickly
Press quickly and lightly at 45 degrees over the tender area, then withdraw slowly
Tap the abdominal wall with the fingertips while the client breathes deeply
Press slowly in all four quadrants for 5 minutes before withdrawing
qs.e: The client is asked about tenderness first, and the test is done away from the tender area. Quick withdrawal with pain on release is the positive finding.

qs.q: A positive rebound tenderness test (pain on quick withdrawal) indicates:
c: Peritoneal irritation or inflammation
Increased intestinal motility
A normal finding in thin clients
Paralytic ileus
qs.e: Normally there is no pain when the hand is withdrawn. Pain on release signals peritoneal irritation or inflammation and should be documented and reported.

qs.q: The abdominal contour is normally documented as:
c: Flat to rounded
Protuberant
Scaphoid
Rounded to protuberant
qs.e: Contour options on the sheet are flat, rounded, scaphoid, and protuberant, but the normal profile from rib margin to pubic bone is flat to rounded.

qs.q: During abdominal inspection of symmetry, asking the client to take a deep breath may help reveal:
c: Masses or enlarged organs
Bowel sounds
Tympany
Striae
qs.e: A deep breath can displace the abdominal organs so that bulging, masses, or enlarged organs become more visible during the symmetry check.

qs.q: In a thin client, an aortic pulsation may be visible in which area during inspection?
c: Epigastric
Right lower quadrant
Left flank
Suprapubic
qs.e: Visible aortic pulsation in the epigastric area can be a normal finding in thin persons; respiratory movement may also be seen.

qs.q: What is the correct client position for an abdominal examination?
c: Supine, arms at sides or across the chest, knees bent or on a pillow
Prone with arms overhead
Upright in high Fowler's with legs straight
Supine with legs straight and arms overhead
qs.e: Supine with knees bent relaxes the abdominal musculature; the client is draped appropriately and comfort is maintained.

qs.q: Which joint type is represented by the skull sutures and permits no movement?
c: Fibrous
Cartilaginous
Synovial
Bursa-type
qs.e: Fibrous joints are non-movable, with skull sutures given as the example. Cartilaginous joints are slightly moveable (vertebrae) and synovial joints are freely moveable.

qs.q: A joint that is slightly moveable and typified by the vertebrae is classified as:
c: Cartilaginous
Fibrous
Synovial
Bursa-type
qs.e: Cartilaginous joints allow slight movement, and the vertebrae are the example given. Use this to sort the three joint types on a matching item.

qs.q: Which statement best describes a synovial joint?
c: Freely moveable; a synovial membrane secretes fluid
Slightly moveable; vertebrae are the example
Non-movable; skull sutures are the example
Non-movable; a synovial membrane secretes fluid
qs.e: Synovial joints are freely moveable and their synovial membrane secretes joint fluid. The other choices describe cartilaginous and fibrous joints.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the range-of-motion documentation categories on the Module 4 sheet?
c: Passive
Full
Active
Limited
qs.e: ROM is charted as Full, Active, or Limited, with a check or X for Right and Left. Passive ROM is performed when active ROM is limited, but it is not a documentation category.

qs.q: If a client demonstrates limitation on active range of motion, the next step is to:
c: Perform passive range of motion
Stop the musculoskeletal exam
Repeat active range of motion three times
Grade muscle strength from 0 to 5
qs.e: Active ROM is done first; if a limitation is found, passive ROM is performed to further characterize it, and movements are compared bilaterally.

qs.q: Turning the forearm so that the palm is up is called:
c: Supination
Pronation
Inversion
Circumduction
qs.e: Supination turns the palm up; pronation turns the palm down. These are two of the movement terms she defined.

qs.q: Moving the sole of the foot inward at the ankle is called:
c: Inversion
Eversion
Adduction
Rotation
qs.e: Inversion turns the sole inward at the ankle; eversion turns the sole outward. Learn the pair as a set.

qs.q: Moving the head around a central axis is called:
c: Rotation
Circumduction
Flexion
Abduction
qs.e: Rotation is movement around a central axis, and the head is the example given. Circumduction is a circular movement of the arm around the shoulder.

qs.q: Which instrument is pictured and used to measure range of motion?
c: Goniometer
Stethoscope
Otoscope
Sphygmomanometer
qs.e: The goniometer is the tool shown for measuring the degree of joint range of motion.

qs.q: Muscle strength is assessed through which maneuver?
c: The same motions used for active range of motion, against opposing force
Passive range of motion only
Palpation of the joint capsule
Percussion of the long bones
qs.e: Strength is tested by having the client perform the AROM motions while you apply opposing force, because this isolates the muscle groups surrounding each joint.

qs.q: A normal muscle strength finding is documented as:
c: Equal bilaterally and fully resisting opposing force
Equal bilaterally with mild crepitation
Limited on the non-dominant side
Always graded 3 of 5
qs.e: Strength should be equal on both sides and the client should fully resist your opposing force, so right and left numeric grades normally match.

qs.q: Which sequence matches the head-to-toe order for range of motion assessment?
c: TMJ, cervical spine, shoulder, elbow, wrist & hand, hip, knee, ankle & foot, spine
Spine, TMJ, shoulder, elbow, wrist & hand, cervical spine, hip, knee, ankle & foot
Hip, knee, ankle & foot, TMJ, cervical spine, shoulder, elbow, wrist & hand, spine
Shoulder, elbow, wrist & hand, hip, knee, ankle & foot, spine, TMJ, cervical spine
qs.e: The head-to-toe approach runs TMJ, cervical spine, shoulder, elbow, wrist & hand, hip, knee, ankle & foot, spine [Slide 35]. ⚠ Conflict: the documentation grid does NOT list the joints in this same pattern — it lists TMJ, Neck, Spine, Shoulders, Elbows, Wrists, Fingers, Hips, Knees, Ankles/Feet [doc sheet p. 585] (spine third, Fingers included); use the Slide 35 sequence for the assessment order.

qs.q: In the Module 4 documentation key, the symbol Ø means:
c: Absent
Abnormal
Within normal defined limits
Not assessed
qs.e: The key defines a check mark as within normal defined limits (WNDL), X as abnormal, and Ø as absent.

qs.q: In the abdominal skin section, striae are documented as:
c: A common pigment change
A type of scar
A sign of hernia
An abnormal pulsation
qs.e: Striae are listed as one common pigment change of abdominal skin, along with nevi and a fine venous network in thin persons.

qs.q: Select all: findings associated with hypoactive or absent bowel sounds.
c: Recent surgery
Peritonitis
Paralytic ileus
Complete obstruction
Increased motility
qs.e: Hypoactive or absent sounds are linked to surgery, peritonitis, paralytic ileus, and complete obstruction. Increased motility is associated with hyperactive sounds instead.

qs.q: Select all: the arteries auscultated for bruits during abdominal assessment.
c: Aorta
Renal
Iliac
Femoral
Carotid
qs.e: Bruits are auscultated over the aorta, renal, iliac, and femoral arteries. The carotid is not part of the abdominal vessel list given.

qs.q: Select all: the overall percussion sounds that may be documented for the abdomen.
c: Tympany
Dullness
Hyperresonance
Crepitation
Borborygmi
qs.e: Overall percussion sound is charted as tympany, dullness, or hyperresonance. Crepitation is a musculoskeletal term and borborygmi relates to bowel sounds.

qs.q: Select all: preparation items listed for the abdominal assessment.
c: Provide good lighting
Have the client empty the bladder
Warm hands and stethoscope; keep fingernails short
Ask about the presence of tenderness first
Place the client prone with arms overhead
qs.e: Preparation covers lighting, a relaxed client with an emptied bladder, warm hands and instrument, short fingernails, and asking about tenderness before palpation. The client is supine, not prone.

qs.q: Select all: the elements you should document about a scar.
c: Cause
Location
Length
Color
Depth
qs.e: Scars are documented for cause, location, and length. The slide's scar list does not include color or depth.

qs.q: Select all: findings noted during inspection of the joints.
c: Skin/tissue color
Swelling
Masses
Deformity
Skin temperature
qs.e: Joint inspection covers size and contour plus color, swelling, masses, and deformity. Skin temperature is assessed by palpation, not inspection.

qs.q: Select all: structures assessed during palpation of the joints.
c: Skin temperature
Surrounding muscles
Bony articulations
Joint capsule
Overall contour
qs.e: Palpation includes skin temperature, muscles, bony articulations, and the joint capsule, and joints are normally non-tender. Size and contour belong to inspection.

qs.q: Select all: findings that should NOT be present during a normal range-of-motion assessment.
c: Tenderness
Pain
Crepitation
Full movement
Bilateral symmetry
qs.e: Normal ROM shows no tenderness, pain, or crepitation. Full movement and bilateral symmetry are expected normal findings.

qs.q: Select all: abnormal abdominal findings you are expected to recognize.
c: Abdominal distention
Hernia
Abnormal bowel sounds
Enlarged organs
Striae
qs.e: The abnormal findings list includes distention, abdominal pain, hernia, abnormal bowel sounds, and enlarged organs. Striae are described as a common pigment change, not an abnormal finding.

qs.q: Select all: the muscle groups given a numeric 0-5 grade on the documentation sheet.
c: Deltoids
Biceps
Quads
Ankles/Feet
TMJ
qs.e: Strength is graded for deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist, fingers, hips, quads, hamstrings, and ankles/feet. TMJ appears in the ROM grid but not in the muscle strength grid.

qs.q: Select all: the terms listed in the Abdomen section of the Module 4 vocabulary list.
c: Aneurysm
Ascites
Hepatomegaly
Splenomegaly
Myalgias
qs.e: The abdominal vocab terms are aneurysm, ascites, borborygmi, bowel sounds, bruit, epigastrium, hepatomegaly, hernia, rebound tenderness, splenomegaly, striae, and tympany. Myalgias is a musculoskeletal term.

qs.q: Auscultation of bowel sounds begins in which quadrant?
qs.e: She directs you to begin in the right lower quadrant and move through all four quadrants, using the diaphragm to judge character and frequency.

qs.q: How many minutes of continuous auscultation are required before you may document bowel sounds as absent?
qs.e: Absence is established only after 5 minutes of continuous auscultation. ⚠ Conflict: [Slide 17] requires listening in all four quadrants before declaring absence, while [Jarvis p. 545] says listening in all four quadrants is not necessary (sounds radiate widely) but agrees on the 5-minute rule; follow her method.

qs.q: Light palpation depresses the abdominal wall approximately how many centimeters?
qs.e: Light palpation goes about 1 cm deep and gives an overall impression of the skin surface and superficial musculature; it is normally soft and smooth.

qs.q: Deep palpation depresses the abdominal wall approximately how many centimeters? Enter a range.
qs.e: Deep palpation goes about 5 to 8 cm and is used to note location, size, consistency, mobility, enlargement, tenderness, and masses.

qs.q: Moving a limb toward the midline of the body is called what?
qs.e: Adduction moves the limb toward the body's midline; its opposite is abduction, which moves the limb away from the midline.

qs.q: Turning the forearm so that the palm is down is called what?
qs.e: Pronation turns the palm down; supination turns the palm up. Learn the two as a matched pair.

qs.q: Moving the sole of the foot outward at the ankle is called what?
qs.e: Eversion turns the sole outward at the ankle, while inversion turns the sole inward.

qs.q: Moving the arm in a circle around the shoulder is called what?
qs.e: Circumduction is the circular movement of the arm around the shoulder joint.

qs.q: Muscle strength is graded on a numeric scale of what? (Muscle Grading Scale p. 587)
qs.e: The grading scale runs 0 to 5, which is six grades. ⚠ Conflict: [Slide 37] calls it a "5-point scale," but [doc sheet] and [Jarvis p. 587] use the numeric 0-5 scale; use 0-5.

qs.q: How many terms are on the Module 4 vocabulary list?
qs.e: The list contains 18 terms: 12 abdominal and 6 musculoskeletal terms.

qs.q: Which measures help prepare a client for an abdominal examination? Select all that apply.
c: Use strong overhead lighting plus a secondary stand light.
Have the client empty the bladder, saving a urine specimen if needed.
Keep the room warm and the client relaxed and comfortable.
Expose the abdomen fully while draping the genitalia and female breasts.
Keep the abdomen covered throughout inspection.
qs.e: Adequate lighting and full abdominal exposure support inspection. Appropriate draping preserves privacy, while warmth, comfort, and an emptied bladder support relaxation.

qs.q: Which approaches are recommended to promote relaxation during abdominal palpation? Select all that apply.
c: Encourage slow breathing.
Use emotive imagery.
Speak in a low, soothing voice.
Use conversation or ask the client to relate the abdominal history.
Ask the client to hold both arms over the head.
qs.e: Slow breathing, imagery, soothing speech, and conversation are distraction techniques that promote relaxation. Arms over the head tense the abdominal musculature.

qs.q: Which positioning and equipment plan best matches the abdominal examination guidance?
c: Supine, head on a pillow, arms at sides or across chest, knees bent or supported; warm hands and stethoscope, short fingernails, and an alcohol wipe for the endpiece.
Supine with arms overhead; use a cool stethoscope to promote relaxation.
Seated with arms overhead; leave the stethoscope endpiece uncleaned.
Supine with arms overhead and knees unsupported; use long fingernails for palpation.
qs.e: The recommended position supports abdominal relaxation, and arms overhead are discouraged because they tense abdominal muscles. Warm hands and equipment, short fingernails, and a cleaned stethoscope endpiece complete the preparation.

qs.q: Which group contains the structures explicitly assigned to the RUQ in the provided Jarvis-based table?
c: Cecum, ileocecal valve area, and appendix region.
Liver edge, gallbladder under the liver border, right kidney lower pole, and ascending colon.
Spleen and left kidney.
Sigmoid colon, full bladder, and gravid uterus.
qs.e: The table names these four structures in the RUQ. Slides 8–10 contain pictures only, so this table is not presented as a complete transcription of the lecture diagrams.

qs.q: Which pairing correctly identifies the RLQ structures and landmarks named in lecture?
c: Sigmoid colon and the lower liver border.
Spleen and the left kidney.
Cecum, ileocecal valve area, and appendix region at McBurney point.
Gallbladder and the pulsatile aorta.
qs.e: The RLQ table includes the cecum, ileocecal valve area, and appendix region at McBurney point. The ileocecal valve area is also the specified starting point for bowel-sound auscultation.

qs.q: Which statement correctly combines LUQ and LLQ findings from the assigned Jarvis pages?
c: The spleen and left kidney are normally palpable; sigmoid tenderness is always abnormal.
The left kidney lies approximately 1 cm below the right; the sigmoid colon is in the RUQ.
The spleen is in the LLQ, and the sigmoid colon is in the LUQ.
The LUQ spleen and left kidney are not normally palpable; the left kidney is about 1 cm higher than the right, and mild sigmoid tenderness in the LLQ may be normal.
qs.e: The source identifies the spleen and left kidney as LUQ structures that are not normally palpable. It places the sigmoid colon in the LLQ and notes that mild tenderness there is normally present.

qs.q: Which landmark statements match the provided anatomy notes? Select all that apply.
c: The xiphoid process and sacral promontory are named landmarks.
The lateral borders of the rectus muscles are named landmarks.
The pulsatile aorta lies in the upper abdomen, slightly left of midline.
A full bladder and gravid uterus are lower-midline structures.
The pulsatile aorta is described as a lower-right-quadrant structure.
qs.e: Jarvis Figure 22.18 names these landmarks and locates the aorta slightly left of midline in the upper abdomen. A full bladder and gravid uterus are located in the lower midline.

qs.q: The abdominal anatomy diagram divides the abdomen into four quadrants and how many regions?
qs.e: Slide 8 presents the four-quadrant and nine-region systems. The supplied slide description does not list the individual region names.

qs.q: Which description correctly explains assessment of abdominal contour?
c: Assess only the umbilicus; normal contour is always scaphoid.
Assess the profile from rib margin to pubic bone from the right side, looking down and then across; normal contour ranges from flat to rounded and reflects nutritional state.
Assess only from the foot of the table; protuberant means the abdomen caves inward.
Assess contour by deep palpation before inspection.
qs.e: Contour describes the abdominal profile and nutritional state; flat to rounded is normal. Jarvis recommends looking down from the right side, then stooping or sitting to look across with the head slightly higher than the abdomen; charting options include flat, rounded, scaphoid, and protuberant.

qs.q: What contour term means that the abdomen caves inward?
qs.e: Scaphoid describes an abdomen that caves inward. In contrast, protuberant describes distention.

qs.q: Which statements or techniques apply to inspection for abdominal symmetry? Select all that apply.
c: Expect bilateral symmetry and note localized bulging, visible masses, or asymmetric shape.
Shine a light across the abdomen toward yourself to highlight small bulges with shadows.
Recheck the abdomen from the foot of the table.
Ask for a deep breath or a sit-up without pushing with the hands.
Assume that localized bulging is the expected symmetric appearance.
qs.e: The abdomen should be bilaterally symmetric. Angled lighting, another viewing position, deep breathing, and a sit-up can make bulges, masses, or enlarged organs easier to see.

qs.q: What term means protrusion of abdominal viscera through an abnormal opening in the muscle wall?
qs.e: A hernia is protrusion of abdominal viscera through an abnormal muscle-wall opening. Inspection may reveal localized bulging.

qs.q: A hard umbilical nodule is identified as a Sister Mary Joseph nodule. Which association is listed in lecture?
c: Dehydration associated with GI disease.
Normal abdominal skin pigmentation.
Metastatic cancer of the stomach, large intestine, ovary, or pancreas.
Normal respiratory movement.
qs.e: A Sister Mary Joseph nodule is a hard umbilical nodule associated with metastatic cancer. The listed primary sites are the stomach, large intestine, ovary, and pancreas.

qs.q: Which umbilical appearance is normal?
c: Midline and inverted, without discoloration, inflammation, or hernia; a piercing site is not red or crusted.
Bluish discoloration around the umbilicus.
A hard umbilical nodule.
An enlarged, everted umbilicus with a hernia.
qs.e: The normal umbilicus is midline and inverted with no discoloration, inflammation, or hernia. A piercing site should not be red or crusted.

qs.q: Which umbilical changes are correctly paired with their associations? Select all that apply.
c: Eversion — ascites or an underlying mass.
Deeply sunken appearance — obesity.
Enlargement and eversion — umbilical hernia; eversion with upward displacement — pregnancy.
Rare bluish periumbilical discoloration, or Cullen sign — intraperitoneal bleeding.
Cullen sign — the expected normal umbilical color.
qs.e: Umbilical position, depth, and color can change with the listed conditions. Cullen sign specifically refers to rare bluish periumbilical discoloration associated with intraperitoneal bleeding.

qs.q: Which description best matches expected abdominal skin findings?
c: An uneven surface with widespread rashes.
Prominent dilated veins in every client.
Redness and crusting as the expected skin appearance.
A smooth, even surface with homogeneous color; common pigmented nevi are circumscribed brown macular or papular areas, while lesions and rashes are normally absent.
qs.e: Normal abdominal skin is smooth and even with homogeneous color. Pigmented nevi, or moles, are common, and the sun-protected abdomen is a useful area for judging pigmentation.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes striae, also called lineae albicantes?
c: They result from intact elastic fibers and remain red indefinitely.
They are linear, jagged marks caused by broken elastic fibers after rapid or prolonged stretching; recent pink or blue marks become silvery-white.
They are pulsatile veins caused only by bowel obstruction.
They are hard umbilical nodules associated with metastatic cancer.
qs.e: Striae follow stretching such as pregnancy or excessive weight gain and may also occur with ascites. Recent striae are pink or blue and later become silvery-white; purple-blue striae are associated with Cushing syndrome.

qs.q: What length range in centimeters is given for striae?
qs.e: The source describes striae as silvery-white, linear, jagged marks measuring 1–6 cm long. Their color also varies with recency and associated conditions.

qs.q: Which abdominal skin findings or assessment conditions are correctly matched? Select all that apply.
c: Glistening, taut skin — ascites.
Redness — localized inflammation.
Natural daylight — best lighting for assessing jaundice.
Purple-blue striae — Cushing syndrome.
Recent pink or blue striae — always a normal fine venous network.
qs.e: Ascites can produce glistening, taut skin, while localized inflammation produces redness. Natural daylight is best for evaluating jaundice, and purple-blue striae are associated with Cushing syndrome.

qs.q: What is the appropriate assessment of an abdominal surgical scar, and why does it matter?
c: Determine its cause and identify its location and length in centimeters; it may alert you to underlying adhesions and excess fibrous tissue.
Ignore it because surgical scars cannot indicate underlying changes.
Assess only its color because location and length are not relevant.
Assume that every scar represents a current hernia.
qs.e: Surgical scars may be present and should be assessed for cause, location, and length. Jarvis also recommends drawing their location in the record because scars can alert the examiner to underlying adhesions and excess fibrous tissue.

qs.q: Which distinction between abdominal venous findings is correct?
c: All visible abdominal veins indicate vena caval obstruction.
Caput medusae is the name for normal silvery-white striae.
A fine venous network can be normal in thin people; prominent dilated veins, or caput medusae, are associated with portal hypertension, cirrhosis, ascites, or vena caval obstruction.
Malnutrition makes abdominal veins less visible.
qs.e: Fine veins may be visible normally in thin people, and malnutrition can make veins more visible. Prominent dilated veins are termed caput medusae and have the listed abnormal associations.

qs.q: Poor skin turgor after pinching and releasing an abdominal skin fold suggests what condition?
qs.e: Turgor is assessed by pinching a skin fold and releasing it. Poor turgor occurs with dehydration, which is common with GI disease.

qs.q: Which visible abdominal movements may be normal?
c: Only marked peristalsis accompanied by distention.
Epigastric aortic pulsations, especially in thin people with relaxed muscle walls; respiratory movement, particularly in males; and occasional peristaltic waves in very thin people.
No visible respiratory movement in any client.
Only a markedly widened aortic pulsation.
qs.e: Normal inspection may reveal epigastric aortic pulsation, respiratory movement, and sometimes peristalsis in very thin people. The degree of movement and accompanying findings matter when distinguishing normal from abnormal.

qs.q: Which conditions are listed with marked aortic pulsation or marked visible peristalsis? Select all that apply.
c: Hypertension with widened pulse pressure — marked aortic pulsation.
Aortic insufficiency or thyrotoxicosis with widened pulse pressure — marked aortic pulsation.
Aortic aneurysm — marked aortic pulsation.
Intestinal obstruction — marked visible peristalsis with distention.
Normal umbilical inversion — marked visible peristalsis with distention.
qs.e: Marked aortic pulsation is associated with widened pulse pressure and aortic aneurysm. Marked visible peristalsis accompanied by distention suggests intestinal obstruction.

qs.q: Adult male abdominal hair distribution is described as a diamond pattern. What pattern is described for adult females?
qs.e: The source lists a diamond pattern for adult males and an inverted triangle for adult females. Hair distribution is another component of abdominal inspection.

qs.q: Which demeanor is expected during a normal abdominal assessment?
c: Constant turning and restlessness.
Absolute stillness with resistance to movement.
Facial grimacing and rapid, uneven respirations.
Relaxation, a benign facial expression, and slow, even respirations.
qs.e: Normal demeanor includes relaxation, a benign expression, and slow, even breathing. Knees flexed with grimacing and rapid, uneven respirations indicate pain.

qs.q: Which comparison of pain behaviors is correct?
c: Restlessness and constant turning suggest colicky pain such as gastroenteritis or bowel obstruction; absolute stillness with resistance to movement suggests peritonitis pain.
Absolute stillness is the characteristic behavior of colicky pain, while constant turning identifies peritonitis.
Both behaviors are described as normal relaxed demeanor.
Neither behavior contributes to abdominal pain assessment.
qs.e: Colicky pain may produce restlessness and repeated turning. Peritonitis pain may cause the person to remain absolutely still and resist movement.

qs.q: Why does the supplied abdominal assessment sequence place auscultation immediately after inspection?
c: Auscultation is intended to increase peristalsis before palpation.
Percussion and palpation eliminate all bowel sounds.
Percussion and palpation can increase peristalsis and falsely alter bowel sounds.
Inspection cannot identify abdominal movement.
qs.e: Auscultation precedes percussion and palpation to avoid stimulating peristalsis and altering bowel sounds. Jarvis notes that early research questions whether this sequence is necessary, but further research is needed.

qs.q: For this instructor's bowel-sound assessment, which technique should you follow?
c: Use firm diaphragm pressure and declare absence after one quiet quadrant.
Use the diaphragm lightly, begin in the RLQ at the ileocecal valve area, auscultate all four quadrants, and listen continuously for 5 minutes before declaring sounds absent.
Listen only in the LUQ and count every sound.
Percuss first and omit the 5-minute listening period.
qs.e: ⚠ Conflict: Slide 17 requires all four quadrants, whereas Jarvis p. 545 says all four are unnecessary because sounds radiate widely; follow the instructor's all-four-quadrant method starting in the RLQ. Both require 5 minutes before declaring absence; light diaphragm pressure avoids stimulating extra sounds, and the ileocecal valve area is described as a site where bowel sounds are always present.

qs.q: Normal bowel sounds occur irregularly within what range per minute?
qs.e: Normal bowel sounds are high-pitched, gurgling, and cascading, occurring irregularly 5–30 times per minute. Jarvis says not to count them but to judge whether they are present, hypoactive, or hyperactive.

qs.q: Which findings or associations match hyperactive bowel sounds? Select all that apply.
c: Loud, high-pitched, rushing, or tinkling sounds caused by increased motility.
Early obstruction.
Gastroenteritis or diarrhea.
Laxative use or subsiding paralytic ileus.
Complete obstruction as the listed cause of increased motility.
qs.e: Hyperactive sounds reflect increased motility and may be loud, rushing, high-pitched, or tinkling. The slide associates them with early obstruction, gastroenteritis, diarrhea, laxatives, and subsiding paralytic ileus.

qs.q: Which conditions are listed as causes of hypoactive or absent bowel sounds? Select all that apply.
c: Abdominal surgery.
Peritonitis.
Paralytic ileus.
Complete obstruction.
Laxative use.
qs.e: The slide lists abdominal surgery, peritonitis, paralytic ileus, and complete obstruction as causes of hypoactive or absent sounds. Laxatives are instead listed with hyperactive sounds.

qs.q: What term names hyperperistalsis commonly described as 'stomach growling'?
qs.e: Borborygmus means hyperperistalsis or stomach growling. It is a fairly common type of hyperactive bowel sound.

qs.q: After colorectal surgery, which interpretation best reflects the source's caution about bowel sounds?
c: Bowel sounds alone reliably establish bowel function.
A silent abdomen is common, so no timed listening is needed.
Oral intake tolerance and stool passage are irrelevant.
Interpretation is subjective; oral intake tolerance, stool passage, and lack of distention may be more reliable indicators of bowel function.
qs.e: Bowel-sound interpretation is highly subjective and may not reliably indicate function. A truly silent abdomen is uncommon, so absence requires the full timed listening period.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe abdominal vascular auscultation? Select all that apply.
c: Listen over the aorta and renal, iliac, and femoral arteries.
Use firmer pressure, especially when assessing a person with hypertension.
Note a sound's location, pitch, and timing.
A systolic bruit is a pulsatile blowing sound associated with stenosis, partial occlusion, or aneurysm; venous hums and peritoneal friction rubs are rare.
A vascular sound is normally required over every abdominal artery.
qs.e: Abdominal vascular auscultation targets the aorta and renal, iliac, and femoral arteries; usually no sound is heard. Characterizing any sound helps distinguish a bruit from other rare sounds.

qs.q: Which description matches the normal bruit that may occur in some healthy people?
c: Present in 4%–20%, usually in people younger than 40; generally from the celiac artery, systolic, medium-to-low pitched, and heard between the xiphoid and umbilicus.
Present in every healthy person and heard only over the femoral arteries.
A high-pitched bowel sound occurring 5–30 times per minute.
A rare blue discoloration around the umbilicus.
qs.e: Although vascular auscultation usually reveals no sound, the source allows a normal bruit in 4%–20% of healthy people, usually those younger than 40. Its typical features are celiac origin, systolic timing, medium-to-low pitch, and location between the xiphoid and umbilicus.

qs.q: Which nasogastric tube placement practice matches the supplied safety guidance?
c: Verify initial placement by auscultating an injected air bolus.
Use abdominal percussion as definitive confirmation.
Confirm placement by chest x-ray; use external tube length measurement and aspirate pH below 5.5 for ongoing checks.
Use bowel-sound frequency as the only ongoing check.
qs.e: Do not use auscultation of an air bolus to verify nasogastric tube placement. The source specifies chest x-ray confirmation and ongoing external-length and aspirate-pH checks.

qs.q: Which set correctly matches abdominal percussion sounds with their qualities and causes?
c: Tympany: low and prolonged over solid organs; dullness: musical over air; hyperresonance: medium-pitched over fluid.

Tympany: high-pitched and musical over stomach or intestinal air; dullness: medium intensity, duration, and pitch over solid organs, masses, fluid, adipose tissue, or a distended bladder; hyperresonance: very loud, low-pitched, and long with gaseous distention.
Tympany: a vascular blowing sound; dullness: visible peristalsis; hyperresonance: a skin-color change.
Tympany, dullness, and hyperresonance all have identical qualities and causes.
qs.e: Percussion assesses the relative density of abdominal contents, helps locate organs, and screens for abnormal fluid or masses. Air produces tympany, denser contents produce dullness, and gaseous distention produces hyperresonance.

qs.q: How should general abdominal percussion be performed, and what sound should predominate?
c: Percuss deeply only in the RLQ; expect dullness throughout.
Percuss counterclockwise only over visible masses; expect hyperresonance throughout.
Percuss only the bladder; expect a bruit.
Percuss lightly in all four quadrants, moving clockwise; expect tympany because air rises to the surface when supine.
qs.e: Jarvis recommends light, clockwise percussion in all four quadrants to assess prevailing tympany versus dullness. Tympany normally predominates because air rises toward the surface in the supine position.

qs.q: Which plan follows the source's limits on using percussion for organ assessment?
c: Avoid percussion for liver span, splenomegaly, and bladder distention; assess the liver and spleen by palpation and bladder distention with bedside bladder scanning ultrasound.
Use liver percussion because it consistently overestimates true size and has little examiner variability.
Use splenic percussion because it is described as more reliable than palpation.
Use bladder percussion because it is described as definitive.
qs.e: Slides and Jarvis do not recommend these percussion applications: liver percussion can underestimate size, vary between examiners, and miss hepatomegaly. Placing the upper border too low or lower border too high reduces estimated liver span; splenic palpation is more reliable, and bedside ultrasound replaces unreliable bladder percussion.

qs.q: Which description correctly explains costovertebral angle tenderness testing?
c: Directly press the umbilicus; sharp pain is expected.
Strike the abdomen with the diaphragm of the stethoscope.
Place one hand over the 12th rib at the back's CVA and thump it with the ulnar edge of the other fist; a painless thud is normal, while sharp pain suggests kidney or perinephric inflammation.
Percuss the RLQ to determine whether the left kidney is palpable.
qs.e: This is indirect fist percussion for kidney tenderness, with pyelonephritis given as an example of an inflammatory cause of sharp pain. It is usually performed during thoracic assessment with the client seated and the examiner behind.

qs.q: Which description correctly compares the advanced-practice ascites percussion tests?
c: A fluid wave needs no midline hand, and shifting dullness reliably detects all volumes below 500 mL.

For a fluid wave, a firm midline hand blocks skin transmission and a distinct tap after striking the opposite flank is positive; for shifting dullness, mark the supine tympany-to-flank-dullness level, roll the person right, and look for an upward shift.
A positive fluid wave excludes large ascites, and shifting dullness replaces ultrasound as the definitive test.
Both tests assess only gaseous distention and do not assess fluid.
qs.e: A positive fluid wave indicates large ascites, and shifting dullness also requires large volumes, failing to detect volumes below the stated 500–1100 mL range. Ultrasound is the definitive tool.

qs.q: Which statements describe the purposes and precautions of abdominal palpation? Select all that apply.
c: Assess the size, location, and consistency of certain organs.
Screen for abnormal masses or tenderness.
Ask about tenderness and assess painful areas last to avoid muscle guarding.
Observe nonverbal cues of discomfort.
Begin with the most painful area to promote relaxation.
qs.e: Palpation assesses selected organ characteristics and screens for masses and tenderness. Asking about pain, leaving tender areas until last, and watching nonverbal cues help avoid provoking guarding and recognize discomfort.

qs.q: Approximately how far should the abdominal wall be depressed during light palpation?
qs.e: Light palpation depresses the wall approximately 1 cm to form an overall impression of the skin surface and superficial musculature, not to search for organs. Note increased resistance, muscle guarding, and tenderness.

qs.q: Which muscle-strength grading range should you use for this course?
c: 1–5, comprising five grades.
0–4, comprising five grades.
1–6, comprising six grades.
0–5, comprising six grades.
qs.e: ⚠ Conflict: Slide 37 calls this a '5-point scale,' but the instructor's documentation sheet and Jarvis specify grades 0–5, which comprise six grades. Use 0–5.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe abdominal palpation? Select all that apply.
c: It assesses the size, location, and consistency of certain organs.
It screens for abnormal masses and tenderness.
Tender areas should be assessed first.
Nonverbal discomfort cues should be observed.
Light palpation normally finds a soft, smooth abdomen.
qs.e: Palpation assesses organs and screens for masses or tenderness. Assess tender areas last so pain or rigidity does not obscure subsequent palpation.

qs.q: Approximately how many centimeters should the abdominal wall be depressed during light palpation?
qs.e: Light palpation forms an overall impression of the skin surface and superficial musculature rather than searching for organs. Note increased resistance, guarding, and tenderness.

qs.q: Which technique correctly describes light abdominal palpation?
c: Separate all five fingers and drag them counterclockwise.
Keep the first four fingers together, use gentle rotary movements with skin and fingers moving together, lift rather than drag, and proceed clockwise.
Use the fingertips to press 5–8 cm at each location.
Keep the skin stationary while rapidly sliding the fingers across it.
qs.e: Light palpation uses the first four fingers together and gentle rotary movement at about 1 cm depth. Lifting rather than dragging and proceeding clockwise follows the described technique.

qs.q: Which measures help relax a patient before or during abdominal palpation? Select all that apply.
c: Bend the knees and keep the palpating hand low and parallel to the abdomen.
Encourage slow breathing in through the nose and out through the mouth.
Use a low, soothing voice and emotive imagery.
For ticklish patients, place their hand beneath yours with your fingers curled over theirs, or palpate around/with the stethoscope immediately after auscultation.
Keep the knees straight and assess painful areas first.
qs.e: These measures reduce tension and ticklishness during palpation. The hand-under-hand method uses the observation that people are not ticklish to themselves.

qs.q: Which comparison correctly distinguishes voluntary guarding from involuntary rigidity?
c: Voluntary guarding is constant and boardlike; involuntary rigidity relaxes on exhalation.
Both findings always disappear with slow breathing.
Voluntary guarding is bilateral and relaxes slightly on exhalation; involuntary rigidity is constant, boardlike, and may be unilateral.
Involuntary rigidity occurs only when the patient is ticklish.
qs.e: Cold, tension, or ticklishness can cause voluntary guarding, which calls for relaxation measures. Involuntary rigidity protects against acute peritoneal inflammation, and the same area hurts when the person attempts a sit-up.

qs.q: What is the recommended depth in centimeters for deep abdominal palpation?
qs.e: Deep palpation depresses the wall 5–8 cm, or 2–3 inches, while moving clockwise over the entire abdomen. It delineates organs and masses and assesses enlargement, tenderness, location, size, consistency, and mobility.

qs.q: For a very large or obese patient, how should bimanual deep palpation be performed?
c: Stack the hands; the top hand pushes and the bottom hand palpates.
Stack the hands; the bottom hand pushes and the top hand palpates.
Use one hand only and avoid deep pressure.
Place one hand in each lower quadrant and pull outward.
qs.e: The bimanual technique is recommended for very large or obese patients. Stacked hands separate the pushing function of the upper hand from the sensing function of the lower hand.

qs.q: Which statements about tenderness and palpable masses are supported? Select all that apply.
c: Mild tenderness over the sigmoid colon in the LLQ can be normal; other tenderness should be investigated.
A mass should be characterized by location, size, and shape.
Consistency and surface should be described, such as soft/firm/hard and smooth/nodular.
Mobility, including movement with respirations, pulsatility, and tenderness should be assessed.
Every normally palpable abdominal structure is abnormal.
qs.e: Some abdominal structures are normally palpable, and mild sigmoid tenderness is a stated normal exception. A mass requires characterization of its dimensions, texture, movement, pulsation, and tenderness.

qs.q: Which description correctly combines liver palpation technique and normal findings?
c: Support the left lower ribs and palpate the LUQ; a soft mass should descend on exhalation.
Support the back at the right 11th–12th ribs with the left hand; place the right hand in the RUQ parallel to the midline, press under the costal margin, and advance 1–2 cm with each exhalation.
Place both hands over the umbilicus and expect a lateral pulsation.
Begin over the RLQ and expect the liver to be palpable in every adult.
qs.e: The supporting hand lifts the liver toward the palpating hand. A normal liver may be unpalpable or feel like a firm, regular ridge bumping the fingertips on inhalation.

qs.q: An adult's liver is felt more than 1–2 cm below the right costal margin. Which interpretation is supported?
c: This always proves enlargement, regardless of diaphragm position.
This is never significant if the edge is firm.
This suggests enlargement unless the diaphragm is depressed; chronic emphysema can displace a normal-sized liver downward.
This establishes an abdominal aortic aneurysm.
qs.e: A liver extending more than 1–2 cm below the margin suggests enlargement, with depressed diaphragm as an exception. Record the distance, consistency, and tenderness; a firm enlarged liver may indicate cirrhosis.

qs.q: Which description correctly pairs alternative liver assessment methods with their techniques?
c: Hooking: fingers over the costal margin from above during a deep breath; scratch test: stethoscope at the xiphoid while stroking upward along the midclavicular line from the RLQ.
Hooking: fingers beneath the left flank; scratch test: stethoscope over the bladder.
Hooking: rapid release from the LLQ; scratch test: assess pain on inspiration.
Hooking: press over the aorta; scratch test: compare lateral pulsations.
qs.e: In the scratch test, sound is magnified at the liver edge. It is useful when distention, obesity, tenderness, or guarding limits assessment.

qs.q: The adult spleen generally must reach how many times its normal size before it can be palpated?
qs.e: The adult spleen is normally not palpable and must be enlarged to approximately three times normal size to be felt. If an enlarged spleen is felt, stop palpating and refer because it is friable and ruptures easily; describe its distance below the costal margin.

qs.q: Which statements about assessing the spleen are supported? Select all that apply.
c: Lift behind the left 11th–12th ribs with the left hand and place the right hand obliquely in the LUQ, fingers toward the left axilla.
Push under the left costal margin during a deep breath; rolling onto the right side is an alternative.
Splenic enlargement can accompany mononucleosis, trauma, leukemia/lymphomas, portal hypertension, or HIV.
Fever plus travel should prompt consideration of malaria.
Continue repeated deep palpation after an enlarged spleen is detected.
qs.e: The described positioning brings the spleen toward the examiner's fingers. The listed conditions can accompany enlargement, but detection of an enlarged spleen calls for stopping palpation and referral.

qs.q: Which kidney assessment finding is correctly described?
c: Both adult kidneys must be palpable.
The left kidney is 1 cm lower than the right and normally palpable.
Duck-bill hands at the flank, firm pressure, and a deep breath may reveal the right kidney as a round, smooth mass sliding between the fingers; the left is 1 cm higher and normally not palpable.
A normal kidney produces widened lateral pulsations.
qs.e: The right kidney is occasionally palpable as a normal finding. The left kidney sits higher and is not normally palpable in the adult.

qs.q: What is the normal palpable width of the abdominal aorta in centimeters?
qs.e: Assess with opposing thumb and fingers in the upper abdomen slightly left of midline; normal pulsation is anterior. Widened lateral pulsation pushing the fingers apart suggests an aneurysm, but palpation accuracy is poor because of skin, adipose tissue, and the aorta's retroperitoneal position.

qs.q: Which technique and interpretation correctly describe rebound tenderness?
c: Quickly press over the painful site and release slowly; pain on release is normal.
At the end of the examination, slowly press deeply at 90° in an area remote from pain, then withdraw quickly; pain on release suggests peritoneal inflammation.
Perform it first over the most tender area; absence of pain suggests appendicitis.
Press lightly and maintain pressure while the patient performs a sit-up.
qs.e: Normal rebound testing causes no pain on withdrawal. Pain on release suggests peritoneal irritation or inflammation, such as appendicitis; localized cough tenderness also signals peritoneal irritation.

qs.q: According to this study guide, RLQ rebound produced by LLQ pressure is called what sign?
qs.e: The supplied guide labels this finding Blumberg sign. It may indicate appendicitis and calls for referral for CT.

qs.q: With fingers beneath the liver border, a patient develops sharp pain and abruptly stops inspiration midway through a deep breath. What does this indicate?
c: Positive Murphy sign, suggesting cholecystitis.
Positive obturator test, suggesting an irritated obturator muscle.
Normal inspiratory movement of the liver.
Positive iliopsoas test, suggesting an inflamed appendix.
qs.e: Murphy sign is inspiratory arrest associated with sharp pain and suggests cholecystitis. It is less accurate in patients older than 60 years, among whom 25% have no abdominal tenderness.

qs.q: Where is McBurney point, and what does maximal tenderness there suggest?
c: At the xiphoid; cholecystitis.
At the left costal margin; splenic enlargement.
1.5–2 inches from the anterior superior iliac spine along the line toward the umbilicus; appendicitis.
At the umbilicus; normal sigmoid tenderness.
qs.e: McBurney point lies along the line from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. Maximal tenderness at this point is associated with appendicitis.

qs.q: Which comparison correctly describes the iliopsoas and obturator tests?
c: Both require pressing under the liver during inspiration.
Iliopsoas: resist downward pressure on the distal thigh with the straight right leg raised while supine; obturator: flex the right hip and knee 90° and rotate internally/externally.
Iliopsoas: rotate the flexed left leg; obturator: withdraw abdominal pressure rapidly.
Both are positive only when no pain occurs.
qs.e: RLQ pain with the iliopsoas test suggests an inflamed or perforated appendix. Pain with the obturator test suggests an inflamed appendix irritating the obturator muscle; this test is less specific.

qs.q: Which Alvarado (MANTRELS) score assignments and thresholds are correct? Select all that apply.
c: Migration to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, and nausea/vomiting each earn 1 point.
RLQ tenderness and leukocytosis above 10,000/µL each earn 2 points.
Rebound and oral temperature ≥37.3°C each earn 1 point.
A left shift with >75% neutrophils earns 1 point.
Oral temperature ≥37.3°C earns 2 points, and RLQ tenderness earns 1 point.
qs.e: MANTRELS totals 10 points across these eight components. RLQ tenderness and leukocytosis are the two components worth 2 points each.

qs.q: How should Alvarado scores of 4 and 7 be interpreted?
c: Both exclude appendicitis.
Both confirm appendicitis.
A score of 4 increases probability; 7 decreases it.
A score of 4 significantly decreases the probability of appendicitis; 7 increases it.
qs.e: A score ≤4 significantly decreases the probability of appendicitis, whereas a score ≥7 increases it. These are probability thresholds rather than statements of certainty.

qs.q: What term means protrusion of an abdominal viscus through an abnormal opening in the muscle wall?
qs.e: A hernia is protrusion of an abdominal viscus through an abnormal muscle-wall opening. Slide 27 lists hernia alongside distention, pain, abnormal bowel sounds, and enlarged organs as abnormal abdominal findings.

qs.q: Which comparison correctly distinguishes distention from obesity versus air or gas?
c: Obesity produces a uniformly rounded abdomen with a sunken umbilicus and tympany with scattered dullness over fat; air/gas produces a single round curve with broad tympany and possible muscle spasm.
Obesity produces an everted umbilicus and a positive fluid wave; air/gas produces a ropelike mass.
Both always produce localized distention and dullness over a solid mass.
Air/gas produces fetal heart tones; obesity produces shifting dullness.
qs.e: Obesity produces uniform rounding, and palpation may be normal or difficult through the wall. Air or gas produces tympany over a large area, sometimes with muscle spasm.

qs.q: A patient has a single abdominal curve, everted umbilicus, bulging flanks, taut glistening skin, increased girth, tympany on top, and dullness over fluid. Which cause best matches?
c: Feces.
Ascites.
Air or gas.
Tumor.
qs.e: Ascites produces this pattern, with a fluid wave and shifting dullness; the taut wall limits palpation. The supplied clinical case similarly describes distention, an everted umbilicus, bulging flanks, dome tympany, flank dullness, shifting dullness, and a positive fluid wave, along with dilated veins, bowel sounds, and no vascular sounds.

qs.q: Which finding favors a large ovarian cyst rather than ascites in the supplied comparison?
c: A fluid wave alone.
Shifting dullness alone.
A lower-half curve toward the midline with an everted umbilicus and transmission of aortic pulsation.
Dullness over fluid alone.
qs.e: A large ovarian cyst can produce dullness over fluid, a fluid wave, and shifting dullness, as can ascites. The table distinguishes the cyst by its lower abdominal contour and transmission of aortic pulsation, which ascites does not transmit.

qs.q: Which remaining abdominal distention patterns are correctly matched? Select all that apply.
c: Pregnancy: single curve, protruding umbilicus, and engorged breasts.
Pregnancy: fetal heart tones, dullness over the uterus, and palpable uterine fundus or fetal parts/movements.
Feces: localized distention, predominant tympany with scattered dullness, and a plastic or ropelike mass.
Tumor: localized distention and dullness if the mass reaches the skin surface; define borders versus an organ.
Feces: diffuse fluid wave with no palpable mass.
qs.e: Pregnancy has uterine and fetal findings in addition to its contour changes. Feces and tumors can both cause localized distention, but their percussion and palpation findings differ.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe abnormal bowel sounds and their associations? Select all that apply.
c: Hyperactive sounds are loud, high-pitched, rushing, or tinkling and indicate increased motility.
Early obstruction, gastroenteritis, and diarrhea can cause hyperactive sounds.
Laxatives and subsiding paralytic ileus can cause hyperactive sounds.
Abdominal surgery, peritonitis, paralytic ileus, and complete obstruction can produce hypoactive or absent sounds.
Complete obstruction is listed only as a cause of hyperactive sounds.
qs.e: Hyperactive sounds accompany increased motility and the listed early or resolving conditions. Hypoactive or absent sounds occur with the listed conditions that reduce bowel activity, including complete obstruction.

qs.q: Which clinical pattern best matches intestinal obstruction?
c: Prior abdominal surgery with adhesions, vomiting, fever, no stool or gas, colicky pain, restlessness, distention, tenderness, and hyperactive sounds early progressing to hypoactive or silent sounds late.
A soft, painless abdomen with unchanged bowel sounds and no vomiting.
Only mild sigmoid tenderness with normal stool passage.
An isolated sunken umbilicus without symptoms.
qs.e: The supplied obstruction portrait combines this history with an ill appearance and progressive bowel-sound changes. Prior abdominal surgery with adhesions is a listed historical clue.

qs.q: Which complications and test findings fit intestinal obstruction?
c: Decreased pulse, increased BP, warm skin, and radiologic gas only distal to the obstruction.
Increased pulse, decreased BP, cool skin, dry mucous membranes; laboratory assessment for dehydration, electrolyte loss, and sepsis; fluid and gas proximal to the obstruction on radiology.
No risk of hypovolemic shock and no laboratory abnormalities.
Only enlarged organs, without fluid or gas accumulation.
qs.e: Obstruction can be accompanied by hypovolemic shock, with increased pulse, decreased blood pressure, cool skin, and dry mucous membranes. The guide lists laboratory evaluation for dehydration, electrolyte loss, and sepsis and radiologic fluid and gas proximal to the obstruction.

qs.q: Which bowel-sound assessment method should you use for this instructor's quiz?
c: Listen only in the LLQ for 1 minute before declaring sounds absent.
Listen in all four quadrants, beginning in the RLQ, and auscultate continuously for 5 minutes before declaring sounds absent.
Listen in any single quadrant for 30 seconds.
Listen for 5 minutes in each quadrant as a required total of 20 minutes.
qs.e: ⚠ Conflict: The instructor's method requires all four quadrants starting in the RLQ, whereas Jarvis says four-quadrant auscultation is not necessary. Follow her method and listen continuously for 5 minutes before declaring bowel sounds absent.

qs.q: What numeric range should be used for muscle-strength grading?
qs.e: ⚠ Conflict: Slide 37 calls this a "5-point scale," but the instructor's doc sheet and Jarvis specify grades 0–5, which are six grades. Use 0–5.

qs.q: Which infant abdominal contour and superficial-vein findings are expected or concerning?
c: A protuberant abdomen reflects immature musculature; a scaphoid abdomen suggests dehydration; a fine superficial venous pattern can be normal in lightly pigmented children until puberty.
A scaphoid abdomen is expected, and a protuberant abdomen always indicates obstruction.
Any superficial vein in infancy is abnormal.
A protuberant abdomen indicates mature musculature.
qs.e: Immature abdominal musculature accounts for the infant's protuberant contour. Scaphoid contour suggests dehydration, while fine superficial veins can remain normal through childhood until puberty in lightly pigmented children.

qs.q: At birth, how many arteries and veins should the umbilical cord contain?
qs.e: The cord is white at birth and contains two arteries and one vein in Wharton's jelly. A cord with only one artery is associated with risk for congenital defects.

qs.q: Which umbilical cord healing timeline is correct?
c: Dries by 3–4 weeks, falls off by 6 years, and never becomes skin-covered.
Dries in a week, falls off by 10–14 days, and is covered by skin by 3–4 weeks.
Falls off at birth and is skin-covered within 24 hours.
Dries at 1 month and falls off at 1 year.
qs.e: The supplied sequence is drying within a week, separation by 10–14 days, and skin coverage by 3–4 weeks. These are distinct stages of normal cord healing.

qs.q: Which statements about infant umbilical hernia and diastasis recti are correct? Select all that apply.
c: An umbilical hernia appears at 2–3 weeks and is most prominent during crying.
An umbilical hernia reaches its maximum at about 1 month, up to 2.5 cm or 1 inch, and usually disappears by 1 year.
Refer an umbilical hernia larger than 2.5 cm; asymptomatic hernias may be monitored until 4–5 years.
Diastasis recti is a midline bulge caused by separated rectus muscles, is more common in Black infants, and warrants referral if it lasts beyond 6 years.
Diastasis recti means protrusion of the spleen through the umbilical cord.
qs.e: Umbilical hernia has the stated appearance, size, and follow-up milestones. Diastasis recti is separation of the rectus muscles producing a midline bulge, rather than the described cord protrusion.

qs.q: Which infant auscultation and percussion findings are expected?
c: Vascular sounds without bowel sounds; dullness over the stomach.
Metallic-tinkling bowel sounds only, no vascular sounds, tympany over the stomach, and dullness over the liver and bladder, which may extend to the umbilicus.
Absent bowel sounds with tympany over the bladder.
Only vascular sounds and uniform dullness.
qs.e: The infant assessment lists bowel sounds described as metallic tinkling, with no vascular sounds. Stomach gas produces tympany, while the liver and bladder produce dullness.

qs.q: Which infant palpation techniques and findings are supported? Select all that apply.
c: Flex the knees and offer a pacifier if the infant is crying.
The abdomen should be soft and supple.
The liver edge at or 1–2 cm below the right costal margin can be normal.
The spleen tip, both kidneys, bladder, cecum, and sausage-like sigmoid in the left inguinal area may be palpable.
A palpable spleen tip in an infant always has the same interpretation as an enlarged palpable adult spleen.
qs.e: Infant palpation uses flexed knees and calming measures, with a normally soft, supple abdomen. Several structures that are not usually palpable in adults may be felt in infants.

qs.q: What is the name of the greenish-black first stool expected within 24 hours after birth?
qs.e: Meconium is the greenish-black first stool expected within 24 hours. By day 4, breastfed stool is golden yellow, pasty, and sour-milk smelling, while formula-fed stool is brown-yellow, firmer, and fecal smelling.

qs.q: Which child abdominal contour progression is correct?
c: Before age 4, the abdomen is flat in every position; after age 4 it is scaphoid.
Before age 4, the abdomen is protuberant supine and standing; after age 4, a potbelly occurs only while standing because of lumbar lordosis, with a flat abdomen supine.
A scaphoid contour is the expected school-age finding.
School-age children normally have a persistently distended abdomen.
qs.e: The child's contour changes with age and position, and school-age children have a slim abdomen. A scaphoid abdomen in a child suggests dehydration or malnutrition.

qs.q: A child younger than 7 years has no abdominal movement with respirations. What does the supplied guide associate with this finding?
c: Expected adolescent development.
Normal lumbar lordosis.
Peritoneal inflammation.
Normal redistribution of body fat.
qs.e: Respirations remain abdominal until 7 years of age. Absence of abdominal respirations before that age is associated with peritoneal inflammation.

qs.q: Which approaches and findings are appropriate when assessing children or adolescents? Select all that apply.
c: Palpate a young child on a parent's lap with knees flexed and head slightly raised; rest a flat palm first and ask the child to pant like a dog.
A child's liver edge 1–2 cm below the costal margin can be normal, and spleen edges and kidney tips are commonly felt.
Because young children often answer yes to pain, observe cry-pitch changes, grimacing, moving away, and guarding.
Respect adolescent sensitivity to exposure with adequate draping or their own clothing; findings are the same as in adults.
Use a young child's yes response as the sole objective evidence of pain.
qs.e: Positioning and gradual contact support the child's examination, while objective behaviors help assess pain. Normal palpability differs from adults in younger children, whereas adolescent findings match adult findings and privacy remains important.

qs.q: Which abdominal changes are expected with aging?
c: Fat shifts toward the extremities, and the abdominal muscles become thicker.
Subcutaneous fat increases over the abdomen and hips as it redistributes away from the extremities; muscles become thinner and less toned, and peristalsis may be visible without obesity.
All visible peristalsis is listed as abnormal in older adults.
The abdominal wall becomes too thick for any organ to be palpable.
qs.e: Aging combines central fat redistribution with thinner, less toned musculature. In the absence of obesity, peristalsis may be visible through the thinner wall.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes palpation and acute abdominal symptoms in aging adults?
c: Organs become harder to palpate, and acute abdominal rigidity is more common.
Kidneys cannot be palpated, and pain is always greater than in younger patients.

Organs are easier to palpate through the thinner wall; the liver edge may be at or just below the costal margin, or 1–2 cm below during inhalation with a depressed diaphragm, while acute abdominal rigidity and reported pain may be less prominent.
Any liver edge at the costal margin proves enlargement.
qs.e: The thinner wall makes organs, including kidneys, easier to palpate. Aging adults have less frequent rigidity with an acute abdomen and often report less pain than younger patients.

qs.q: An adult has constant boardlike abdominal hardness, a large palpable mass, and tenderness. How should these findings be classified in this source?
c: Expected normal findings because some structures are palpable.
Abnormal findings; involuntary boardlike rigidity is associated with acute peritoneal inflammation.
Voluntary guarding that must disappear completely on exhalation.
A normal age-related pattern in every adult.
qs.e: The guide identifies rigidity, large masses, and tenderness as abnormal findings. Constant boardlike involuntary rigidity is associated with acute peritoneal inflammation rather than ordinary voluntary guarding.

qs.q: How may an acute abdomen present differently in an aging patient compared with a younger patient?
c: Abdominal rigidity is less common, and the patient often reports less pain.
Abdominal rigidity is more common, and the patient often reports more pain.
Abdominal rigidity is less common, but the patient always reports more pain.
Abdominal rigidity and pain are always absent.
qs.e: In aging patients, abdominal rigidity with an acute abdomen is less common, and reported pain is often less than in younger patients. Less pain does not contradict the presentation described in lecture.

qs.q: Which findings appear in the Jarvis abdominal case's objective description? Select all that apply.
c: Distended abdomen with an everted umbilicus, bulging flanks, and prominent dilated veins
Bowel sounds present and no vascular sounds
Tympany at the abdominal dome, flank dullness, shifting dullness, and a positive fluid wave
Firm, nodular, nontender liver
Retracted umbilicus, flat flanks, and a soft, tender liver
qs.e: The case combines visible abdominal changes, present bowel sounds without vascular sounds, the listed percussion and fluid findings, and a firm, nodular, nontender liver. These are the case's objective findings, not a list of universally normal findings.
