qs.q: Which abdominal assessment technique–finding pairings match the source? Select all that apply.
c: Inspection: contour, symmetry, umbilicus, pulsations, and skin
Auscultation: bowel sounds described as present, hyperactive, or hypoactive
Percussion: overall sound
Light palpation: smoothness, softness, rigidity, guarding, and tenderness
Auscultation: liver firmness and nodularity
qs.e: The source assigns visible features to inspection, bowel sounds to auscultation, overall sound to percussion, and texture or tenderness findings to light palpation.

qs.q: Which bowel-sound assessment method should you follow for this instructor?
c: Start in the RLQ, auscultate all four quadrants, and listen continuously for 5 minutes before declaring sounds absent.
Start in the RLQ, assess only one quadrant, and declare sounds absent after 1 minute.
Start in the LUQ, auscultate two quadrants, and declare sounds absent immediately if silent.
Auscultate all four quadrants but omit the continuous listening period.
qs.e: ⚠ Conflict: The instructor's method requires all four quadrants starting in the RLQ and 5 minutes of continuous listening before declaring sounds absent; Jarvis differs in stating that assessment of all four quadrants is not necessary. Follow the instructor's method for this quiz.

qs.q: Which statements describe the purpose and functional component of the musculoskeletal assessment? Select all that apply.
c: It assesses joints, muscles, and bones.
It evaluates function for ADLs and screens for abnormalities.
Much ADL information comes from the history.
Useful observations include gait, posture, sitting or rising, removing a jacket, manipulating a pen, and rising from supine.
ADL function is assessed only through isolated joint measurements.
qs.e: The musculoskeletal examination includes both structural assessment and functional assessment. History supplies much ADL information, while ordinary movements during the examination provide additional observations.

qs.q: Which description correctly compares the three joint types?
c: Fibrous: immobile, joined by interjacent fibrous tissue or cartilage, as in skull sutures; cartilaginous: slightly movable, separated by fibrous cartilage, as in vertebrae; synovial: freely movable, with a fluid-secreting synovial membrane lining the enclosing cavity
Fibrous: freely movable; cartilaginous: immobile; synovial: slightly movable
Fibrous: exemplified by vertebrae; cartilaginous: exemplified by skull sutures; synovial: lacks a cavity
Fibrous: fluid-secreting cavity; cartilaginous: freely movable; synovial: bones united without movement
qs.e: Slide 29 distinguishes the types by connecting tissue, mobility, and joint structure. Skull sutures illustrate fibrous joints, vertebrae illustrate cartilaginous joints, and synovial joints have a membrane-lined cavity that secretes fluid.

qs.q: Which actions follow the recommended general musculoskeletal examination approach? Select all that apply.
c: Make the person comfortable and drape to visualize the part being examined.
Proceed head to toe and proximal to distal.
Support joints at rest so muscles remain soft and relaxed; use firm support and gentle movement around inflammation.
Compare corresponding paired joints for symmetry of structure and function.
Leave inflamed joints unsupported and use forceful movement.
qs.e: Comfort, appropriate exposure, an orderly examination, and joint support facilitate assessment. Corresponding joints should be compared because symmetry of structure and function is expected.

qs.q: Which examination is sufficient for most people?
c: A screening examination integrating joint inspection and palpation into body-region assessment, observing ROM during movement, and including age-specific screening
A complete musculoskeletal examination regardless of symptoms or function
Only a muscle-strength examination
Only an ADL history without examination observations
qs.e: A screening examination suffices for most people. It combines regional inspection and palpation, observed ROM, and age-specific screening.

qs.q: Which set of indications calls for a complete musculoskeletal examination?
c: Articular disease, musculoskeletal symptoms, or ADL problems
Only a desire to measure every joint in an otherwise asymptomatic person
Only normal gait and normal posture
Only symmetric joint structure and function
qs.e: Jarvis recommends a complete examination for articular disease, musculoskeletal symptoms, or problems with ADLs. Most other people can receive a screening examination.

qs.q: Which statements about joint inspection are correct? Select all that apply.
c: Inspect the size and contour of every joint.
Inspect overlying skin and tissue for color, swelling, masses, and deformity.
Swelling is significant and signals joint irritation.
Use the contralateral side for comparison.
Swelling should be ignored when joint color is unchanged.
qs.e: Joint inspection includes both joint shape and the condition of overlying tissues. Swelling signals irritation, and the opposite side provides a comparison.

qs.q: Which are listed causes of joint-area swelling? Select all that apply.
c: Excess joint fluid, called effusion
Thickening of the synovial lining
Inflammation of surrounding soft tissue, including bursae or tendons
Bony enlargement
Normal discrete cracking from a tendon slipping over bone
qs.e: The listed causes include fluid accumulation, thickened synovium, surrounding soft-tissue inflammation, and bony enlargement. A discrete tendon or ligament crack is discussed separately from these swelling mechanisms.

qs.q: Which set correctly defines the listed musculoskeletal deformities?
c: Fracture: bone break; dislocation: complete loss of bone contact; subluxation: contact retained with abnormal alignment; contracture: muscle shortening limiting ROM; ankylosis: joint stiffness or fixation
Fracture: muscle shortening; dislocation: retained contact with abnormal alignment; subluxation: complete loss of contact; contracture: bone break; ankylosis: free movement
Fracture: joint fixation; dislocation: bone break; subluxation: muscle shortening; contracture: full ROM; ankylosis: excess fluid
Fracture: excess fluid; dislocation: slight misalignment with contact; subluxation: normal alignment; contracture: synovial thickening; ankylosis: normal mobility
qs.e: Dislocation and subluxation differ in whether contact between the bones is completely lost. Fracture concerns bone integrity, contracture concerns muscle shortening, and ankylosis concerns joint stiffness or fixation.

qs.q: Which actions or interpretations belong in joint palpation? Select all that apply.
c: Assess skin temperature, muscles, bony articulations, and the joint capsule area.
Notice heat, tenderness, swelling, and masses.
If tenderness occurs, localize it to skin, muscles, bursae, ligaments, tendons, fat pads, or the joint capsule.
Interpret warmth with tenderness as a signal of inflammation.
Treat tenderness as an expected normal joint finding.
qs.e: Palpation assesses multiple joint and surrounding tissue structures, not just bone. Tenderness is abnormal and should be localized; warmth with tenderness signals inflammation.

qs.q: Which palpation finding suggests a thickened synovial membrane?
c: A doughy or boggy feel
A normally palpable, firm membrane in every joint
A discrete audible crack without any palpable tissue change
A completely absent joint cavity
qs.e: The normal synovial membrane is not palpable. When thickened, it feels doughy or boggy.

qs.q: Which statement correctly interprets joint fluid on palpation?
c: A normal joint contains a small, nonpalpable amount; palpable fluid is abnormal and may shift to produce visible bulging elsewhere in the sac.
Normal joint fluid is always readily palpable and produces visible bulging.
Any joint fluid is abnormal, even when nonpalpable.
Palpable fluid cannot shift within the joint sac.
qs.e: A small amount of joint fluid is normal but cannot normally be palpated. Abnormal palpable fluid can shift and cause bulging on another side of the sac.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe ROM assessment and expected findings? Select all that apply.
c: Begin with active ROM and model the movements for the person.
If movement is limited, gently assess passive ROM with the muscles relaxed.
Compare joints bilaterally; normal active and passive ranges should be the same.
Normal ROM should occur without tenderness, pain, or crepitation.
Begin by forcing every joint through passive ROM before observing voluntary movement.
qs.e: Active ROM is voluntary movement and is assessed first. Passive assessment follows a limitation, while bilateral comparison and the absence of pain, tenderness, and crepitation help establish expected findings.

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes articular from extra-articular disease?
c: Articular disease is inside the capsule, may include arthritis, affects the whole joint, and limits all planes of active and passive ROM; extra-articular disease involves a specific tendon, ligament, or nerve and affects a localized spot and certain planes, especially active motion.
Articular disease affects only one tendon, while extra-articular disease always affects the entire capsule.
Articular disease limits only active motion, while extra-articular disease always limits all passive planes.
Neither type causes swelling or tenderness.
qs.e: Articular disease produces whole-joint swelling and tenderness with limitation across all planes in both active and passive motion. Extra-articular disease produces more localized findings and selectively affects movement, especially active motion.

qs.q: Which finding is crepitation rather than the normal discrete crack described in lecture?
c: Audible and palpable crunching or grating during movement from roughened articular surfaces, as may occur in RA
A single crack when a tendon or ligament slips over bone during a knee bend
Painless, silent movement through full ROM
Visible fluid shifting to the opposite side of a joint sac
qs.e: Crepitation is audible and palpable crunching or grating caused by roughened articular surfaces. It differs from a normal discrete crack caused by a tendon or ligament slipping over bone.

qs.q: Name, in order, the movements that bend a limb at a joint and straighten it at a joint.
qs.e: Flexion bends a limb at a joint. Extension straightens it.

qs.q: What movement extends a body part beyond straight, as when lifting the chin toward the ceiling?
qs.e: Hyperextension is extension beyond straight. The source uses lifting the chin toward the ceiling as an example.

qs.q: Name, in order, movement away from the midline and movement toward the midline.
qs.e: Abduction moves a limb away from the midline. Adduction moves it toward the midline.

qs.q: Name, in order, turning the forearm palm down and turning it palm up.
qs.e: Pronation turns the forearm so the palm faces down. Supination turns it so the palm faces up.

qs.q: Name, in order, turning the sole inward at the ankle and turning it outward.
qs.e: Inversion turns the sole inward at the ankle. Eversion turns it outward.

qs.q: Name, in order, moving the arm in a circle around the shoulder and moving the head or limb around a central axis.
qs.e: Circumduction moves the arm in a circle around the shoulder. Rotation moves the head or a limb around a central axis.

qs.q: What instrument is shown measuring a knee on Slide 34?
qs.e: Slide 34 depicts a goniometer measuring the knee. Jarvis lists it as occasional equipment for the musculoskeletal examination.

qs.q: Which sequence matches Slide 35's head-to-toe ROM approach?
c: TMJ → cervical spine → shoulder → elbow → wrist and hand → hip → knee → ankle and foot → spine
Cervical spine → TMJ → elbow → shoulder → hip → wrist and hand → knee → spine → ankle and foot
Spine → ankle and foot → knee → hip → wrist and hand → elbow → shoulder → cervical spine → TMJ
TMJ → shoulder → wrist and hand → cervical spine → elbow → knee → hip → spine → ankle and foot
qs.e: Slide 35 gives this regional assessment order. The expected degree measurements come from Jarvis; the slides provide motion terms and the order rather than degrees.

qs.q: Which set describes expected TMJ motion?
c: Mouth opens 3–6 cm, approximately three fingers sideways; lateral movement is 1–2 cm; protrusion occurs without deviation.
Mouth opens 1–2 cm; lateral movement is 3–6 cm; protrusion should deviate.
Mouth opens 3–6 cm; lateral movement is absent; protrusion should deviate.
Mouth opens 1 cm; lateral movement is 6 cm; protrusion is not assessed.
qs.e: Expected TMJ assessment includes opening, lateral movement, and protrusion. Opening is 3–6 cm, lateral movement is 1–2 cm, and protrusion should not deviate.

qs.q: What are the expected cervical spine ranges for flexion, hyperextension, lateral bending, and rotation, respectively?
qs.e: Cervical flexion is 45°, hyperextension 55°, lateral bending 40°, and rotation 70°. These are the Jarvis ranges supplied in the study guide.

qs.q: Which set correctly gives shoulder flexion, hyperextension, abduction, adduction, internal rotation, and external rotation, respectively?
qs.e: Shoulder flexion and abduction reach 180°, hyperextension reaches up to 50°, and adduction is 50°. Internal and external rotation are each 90°.

qs.q: Which elbow and forearm findings match the expected ranges and healthy variation in lecture?
c: Flexion 150–160°; extension about 0°, with some healthy people lacking 5–10° or hyperextending 5–10°; the hand touches the table with both pronation and supination.
Flexion 90°; extension always exactly 0°; the hand touches the table only with pronation.
Flexion 130–150°; extension always 15°; pronation and supination are not assessed.
Flexion 180°; any deviation from 0° extension is necessarily abnormal.
qs.e: Expected elbow flexion is 150–160°, and extension is approximately 0°. Jarvis allows 5–10° of extension deficit or hyperextension in some healthy people and describes the hand touching the table in both forearm positions.

qs.q: Which wrist and hand range set matches the source?
c: Wrist hyperextension/palmar flexion 70°/90°; MCP flexion/hyperextension 90°/30°; ulnar/radial deviation 50–60°/20°; abduction 20°; tight fist
Wrist hyperextension/palmar flexion 90°/70°; MCP flexion/hyperextension 30°/90°; ulnar/radial deviation 20°/50–60°; abduction 45°; loose fist
Wrist hyperextension/palmar flexion 45°/20°; MCP flexion/hyperextension 20°/30°; ulnar/radial deviation 70°/90°; abduction 90°; tight fist
Wrist hyperextension/palmar flexion 30°/35°; MCP flexion/hyperextension 70°/40°; ulnar/radial deviation 90°/90°; abduction 50°; loose fist
qs.e: The source lists wrist, MCP, deviation, abduction, and fist findings separately. Correctly associating each number with its movement prevents reversing paired ranges.

qs.q: Which set gives expected hip flexion with the knee straight, flexion with the knee bent, internal rotation, external rotation, abduction, adduction, and hyperextension, respectively?
qs.e: Hip flexion is 90° with the knee straight and 120° with it bent. The remaining ranges are internal rotation 40°, external rotation 45°, abduction 40–45°, adduction 20–30°, and hyperextension 15°.

qs.q: Which knee ROM findings match the source?
c: Flexion 130–150° and extension 0°, with some people hyperextending 15°
Flexion 150–160° and extension 30° in everyone
Flexion 90° and extension 20°, without variation
Flexion 180° and extension 45°
qs.e: The expected knee flexion range is 130–150°, and extension is 0°. The source notes that some people hyperextend 15°.

qs.q: Which ankle and foot assessment matches the expected ranges?
c: Plantar flexion 45°, dorsiflexion 20°, eversion 20°, inversion 30°; assess toe flexion and extension
Plantar flexion 20°, dorsiflexion 45°, eversion 30°, inversion 20°; omit toe movement
Plantar flexion 90°, dorsiflexion 70°, eversion 50°, inversion 50°; assess toe rotation only
Plantar flexion 30°, dorsiflexion 35°, eversion 45°, inversion 90°; omit toe movement
qs.e: The ankle ranges are plantar flexion 45°, dorsiflexion 20°, eversion 20°, and inversion 30°. The source also includes toe flexion and extension without supplying degree values.

qs.q: What are the expected spine ranges for flexion, hyperextension, lateral bending, and rotation, respectively?
qs.e: The spine ranges are flexion 75–90°, hyperextension 30°, lateral bending 35°, and rotation 30° to each side. These differ from the separately listed cervical spine ranges.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe muscle-strength assessment? Select all that apply.
c: Test the prime-mover groups surrounding each joint using the same motions as active ROM.
Ask the person to flex and hold while you apply opposing force.
Expected strength is equal bilaterally and fully resists the examiner's opposing force.
Interpret muscle and joint status together, recognizing that strength varies widely among people.
Assess muscle strength independently of joint status and without resistance.
qs.e: Strength testing repeats active-ROM motions against opposing force. Muscle and joint status are interdependent, and a grading system helps describe strength despite wide variation among people.

qs.q: Which pair correctly describes muscle-strength grades 5 and 4?
c: 5: full ROM against gravity and full resistance, 100%, Normal; 4: full ROM against gravity and some resistance, 75%, Good
5: full ROM against gravity only, 50%, Fair; 4: slight contraction, 10%, Trace
5: full ROM with gravity eliminated, 25%, Poor; 4: no contraction, 0%, Zero
5: full ROM against some resistance, 75%, Good; 4: full resistance, 100%, Normal
qs.e: Grades 5 and 4 both include full ROM against gravity. Full resistance earns grade 5, while some resistance earns grade 4.

qs.q: Which pair correctly describes muscle-strength grades 3 and 2 in the supplied table?
c: 3: full ROM with gravity, 50%, Fair; 2: full ROM with gravity eliminated, labeled passive motion, 25%, Poor
3: full ROM against some resistance, 75%, Good; 2: slight contraction, 10%, Trace
3: full resistance, 100%, Normal; 2: no contraction, 0%, Zero
3: gravity eliminated, 25%, Poor; 2: full ROM with gravity, 50%, Fair
qs.e: Grade 3 indicates full ROM with gravity and is labeled Fair at 50%. Grade 2 indicates full ROM with gravity eliminated, described as passive motion in the supplied table, and is labeled Poor at 25%.

qs.q: Which pair correctly describes muscle-strength grades 1 and 0?
c: 1: slight contraction, 10%, Trace; 0: no contraction, 0%, Zero
1: no contraction, 0%, Zero; 0: slight contraction, 10%, Trace
1: gravity eliminated, 25%, Poor; 0: full ROM with gravity, 50%, Fair
1: some resistance, 75%, Good; 0: full resistance, 100%, Normal
qs.e: Grade 1 requires a slight contraction and is labeled Trace at 10%. Grade 0 indicates no contraction and is labeled Zero at 0%.

qs.q: Which statements describe the recommended spine inspection and expected alignment? Select all that apply.
c: Inspect with the person standing and the gown open at the back.
An imaginary vertical line should run from the head through the spinous processes and gluteal cleft.
Shoulders, scapulae, iliac crests, and gluteal folds should be level, with equal spaces between the arms and lateral thorax.
The side view should show a convex thoracic curve and a concave lumbar curve.
Expected alignment includes unequal arm-to-thorax spaces and a concave thoracic curve.
qs.e: Posterior inspection evaluates straight alignment, level paired landmarks, and equal lateral spaces. The lateral view shows the normal convex thoracic and concave lumbar curves.

qs.q: What is the most sensitive sign of joint disease described in lecture?
qs.e: Limitation in ROM is identified as the most sensitive sign of joint disease. The pattern of limitation helps distinguish articular from extra-articular involvement.

qs.q: Which equipment list matches the musculoskeletal examination source?
c: Tape measure, skin marking pen, and occasionally a goniometer
Goniometer only, with no other equipment listed
Tape measure only, with no skin marking pen
Skin marking pen only, with no measuring equipment
qs.e: Jarvis lists a tape measure and skin marking pen, with a goniometer used occasionally. Slide 34 illustrates the goniometer at the knee.

qs.q: Which age-specific screening pair matches the source?
c: Infants: Ortolani sign; adolescents: scoliosis screening
Infants: scoliosis screening; adolescents: Ortolani sign
Infants and adolescents: Ortolani sign only
Infants and adolescents: no age-specific screening
qs.e: The screening examples are Ortolani sign for infants and scoliosis screening for adolescents. These are included as age-specific components of the screening examination.

qs.q: Which stabilization technique is correct during ROM assessment?
c: During active ROM, stabilize the area proximal to the moving part; during passive ROM, relax the muscles and anchor the joint with one hand while gently moving it to its limit with the other.
During active ROM, leave the proximal area unsupported; during passive ROM, require the muscles to remain contracted.
During passive ROM, use both hands to force movement without anchoring the joint.
Stabilize only after pain occurs and omit muscle relaxation.
qs.e: Proximal stabilization is used while observing active motion. For passive motion, relaxed muscles, joint anchoring, and gentle movement are the specified technique.

qs.q: Select all findings or techniques consistent with normal adult spine inspection and palpation.
c: Inspect standing with the gown open at the back; an imaginary line passes through the head, spinous processes, and gluteal cleft.
Shoulders, scapulae, iliac crests, and gluteal folds are level, and arm-to-lateral-thorax spaces are equal.
The lateral view shows a convex thoracic curve and concave lumbar curve.
Spinous processes are straight and nontender; paravertebral muscles are firm without tenderness or spasm.
Unequal iliac crests and unilateral paravertebral spasm are expected normal findings.
qs.e: Normal inspection emphasizes alignment, symmetry, and the expected lateral curves. Normal palpation finds straight, nontender spinous processes and firm muscles without spasm.

qs.q: Which statement correctly compares kyphosis and lordosis and their associations?
c: Kyphosis is enhanced lumbar concavity; lordosis is enhanced thoracic convexity.

Kyphosis is enhanced thoracic convexity, common with aging or adolescent poor posture; lordosis is pronounced lumbar concavity, associated with obesity, childhood protuberant abdomen, pregnancy, muscular dystrophy, and rickets.
Kyphosis is lateral curvature; lordosis is identified by a unilateral rib hump.
Kyphosis and lordosis both mean loss of all normal spinal curves.
qs.e: Kyphosis exaggerates the thoracic curve, whereas lordosis exaggerates the lumbar curve. Lordosis may be marked with muscular dystrophy and rickets.

qs.q: Unequal shoulder, scapular, and iliac crest levels with a unilateral rib hump during forward bending suggest what lateral spinal curvature?
qs.e: Scoliosis is lateral spinal curvature. Unequal landmark elevation and a rib hump on forward bending are characteristic assessment findings.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe spine ROM assessment?
c: Flexion is 75–90°; lumbar concavity disappears and the back forms a single convex C.
Hyperextension is 30°, lateral bending is 35°, and rotation is 30° bilaterally.
Dots marked on spinous processes during bending should form a straight vertical line on standing; a slight S-shape indicates spinal curvature.
Finish by having the person walk on the toes and then the heels.
Slide 35 supplies all of these numeric spinal ROM values.
qs.e: These spine techniques and ranges come from Jarvis. Slide 35 lists the spine as a ROM region but does not provide these detailed findings.

qs.q: Which pairing correctly distinguishes Phalen testing from the Tinel sign?
c: Phalen: percuss the median nerve; Tinel: hold wrists flexed for 5 minutes.
Phalen: hold hands back to back with wrists flexed 90° for 60 seconds; Tinel: directly percuss the median nerve at the wrist.
Phalen: press the patella against the femur; Tinel: rotate the flexed knee.
Phalen: extend both wrists 30°; Tinel: compare infant knee heights.
qs.e: Phalen reproduces numbness and burning in carpal tunnel syndrome. A positive Tinel sign produces burning or tingling along the nerve distribution and also indicates carpal tunnel syndrome.

qs.q: Which description correctly identifies the bulge sign and its significance?
c: Stroke the medial knee 2–3 times, tap laterally, and watch the medial hollow; a visible fluid wave indicates 4–8 mL of effusion and high risk for knee pain or progressive OA.
Compress the suprapatellar pouch and listen for a meniscal click; this detects 4–8 mL of effusion.
Raise the extended leg and dorsiflex the foot; a fluid wave indicates a herniated disc.
Compare knee heights; a lower knee indicates progressive OA.
qs.e: The bulge sign detects small knee effusions through a visible fluid wave. The source links a positive finding to high risk for knee pain and progressive OA.

qs.q: After compressing the suprapatellar pouch, the examiner sharply pushes the patella against the femur and hears a tap as it contacts the femoral condyles. Name this test.
qs.e: Ballottement of the patella detects larger amounts of knee fluid. A tap as the patella bumps the femoral condyles indicates fluid is present.

qs.q: During a supine examination, the nurse flexes the hip and knee, rotates the leg, applies valgus stress, and slowly extends the knee. A click is felt and heard. What is the correct interpretation and action?
c: Positive Thomas test; document a normal hip.
Positive McMurray test; suspect a torn meniscus and refer to orthopedics.
Positive Tinel sign; suspect carpal tunnel syndrome.
Positive bulge sign; suspect a hip flexion deformity.
qs.e: These maneuvers describe the McMurray test. A felt or heard click suggests a torn meniscus and warrants orthopedic referral.

qs.q: Which sequence and finding correctly describe Lasègue/straight leg raising?
c: Flex one knee to the chest; the opposite thigh lifting indicates a herniated disc.
Raise the extended leg just short of pain, dorsiflex the foot, then raise the unaffected leg; reproduced or worsened sciatic pain, especially with dorsiflexion, suggests a herniated disc.
Raise both flexed knees and compare their heights; equality indicates a herniated disc.
Rotate the flexed knee and listen for a click; a click indicates sciatic pain.
qs.e: Straight leg raising assesses reproduction or worsening of sciatic pain. Pain that worsens with dorsiflexion is the abnormal pattern described for a herniated disc.

qs.q: During the Thomas test, the supine patient brings one knee to the chest while the other leg remains straight. The opposite thigh lifts off the table. What does this indicate?
qs.e: The Thomas test is positive when the opposite thigh lifts from the table. This finding indicates a hip flexion deformity.

qs.q: Which statements about infant hip testing are supported by the assigned text?
c: Ortolani involves adducting and then abducting/lifting the knees; a clunk as the femoral head reseats is positive.
Allis compares knee heights with the knees flexed; one knee lower is positive.
Ortolani is performed at every professional visit until age 1 year.
The assigned Jarvis pages describe Ortolani and Allis for hip dislocation but do not describe the Barlow maneuver.
A clunk during Ortolani is the stated normal finding.
qs.e: Ortolani and Allis assess infant hips using different findings: a reseating clunk versus unequal knee heights. Barlow is explicitly noted as not described in the assigned pages.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes leg-length assessment and imaging guidance?
c: True length is measured from the umbilicus; apparent length is measured from the anterior iliac spine.

True length runs from the anterior iliac spine to the medial malleolus and is equal or within 1 cm; apparent length runs from the umbilicus to the medial malleolus, and Ottawa knee/ankle rules govern imaging referral.
True leg lengths normally differ by 5–8 cm; apparent length is measured to the lateral malleolus.
Equal true lengths exclude pelvic obliquity and hip adduction/flexion deformity.
qs.e: Unequal apparent lengths despite equal true lengths occur with pelvic obliquity or hip adduction/flexion deformity. Ottawa knee/ankle rules guide imaging referral.

qs.q: Which approach correctly supports developmental musculoskeletal assessment?
c: Use only adult strength testing and omit developmental history.
Keep a chart of the usual motor-development sequence and use a questionnaire such as Ages and Stages to screen fine and gross motor skills.
Use Ages and Stages only to measure spinal curvature.
Exclude muscle tone, resting posture, and motor activity because they have no overlap with the neurologic examination.
qs.e: The source recommends tracking the usual motor-development sequence and screening fine and gross motor skills. Muscle tone, resting posture, and motor activity overlap with the neurologic examination.

qs.q: Which infant examination practices and findings are supported by the source?
c: Examine the infant undressed on a warming table; distinguish flexible from fixed positional varus/valgus and check tibial torsion.
Metatarsus adductus usually resolves by age 3 years; assess hips with Ortolani, Allis, and gluteal-fold inspection.
Inspect hands and arms for polydactyly, syndactyly, and a single palmar crease; palpate clavicles because they are the most common birth-fracture site.
Assess equal arm ROM with the Moro reflex; a normal infant wedges securely when lifted under the axillae for strength assessment.
Fixed and flexible foot positions should be treated as indistinguishable findings.
qs.e: Infant assessment includes positional findings, hip screening, hand inspection, clavicle palpation, and age-appropriate movement and strength observations. Flexibility matters when assessing positional varus or valgus.

qs.q: Which infant back findings are correctly described?
c: A single C-curve is normal at birth; a concave cervical curve develops by 2 months as the infant lifts the head prone, and a tuft of hair, dimple, or mass may indicate spina bifida or dermoid sinus.
A concave lumbar curve is the only normal curve at birth; a back dimple excludes abnormalities.
A cervical curve should not appear until age 3 years.
A tuft of hair, dimple, or mass confirms normal muscle strength.
qs.e: The newborn spine normally has a single C-curve, followed by cervical concavity with prone head lifting. A tuft of hair, dimple, or mass warrants concern for the abnormalities named in lecture.

qs.q: Which preschool/school-age assessment statements are correct?
c: Observe spontaneous play; shoulders should be level within 1 cm, scapulae symmetric, and lordosis is common.
Genu varum is normal for 1 year after walking begins; the listed measurement is >2.5 cm between knees with malleoli together.
Genu valgum is normal at 2–3½ years; the listed measurement is >2.5 cm between malleoli with knees together.
Genu varum is assessed with the knees together by measuring the distance between malleoli.
Shoulder asymmetry greater than 5 cm is the stated normal childhood finding.
qs.e: The source distinguishes genu varum and genu valgum by both age and measurement position. Observation during spontaneous play helps assess the child naturally.

qs.q: Which childhood foot and gait statements are supported?
c: Pes planus is normal in infants and resolves by age 3; pronation is common at 12–30 months, but pronation or lack of an arch after age 3 is abnormal.
In-toeing often reflects forefoot adduction and is self-correcting if flexible.
Gait is broad-based at 1–2 years, with narrowing of the base beginning at age 3.
Watch for radial head subluxation at ages 2–4.
A broad-based gait first becomes normal after age 3, and flexible in-toeing never self-corrects.
qs.e: Age and flexibility distinguish expected childhood findings from concerning persistence. The source also highlights radial head subluxation in children ages 2–4.

qs.q: Which plan matches the adolescent assessment guidance?
c: Avoid the adult examination and routinely screen every asymptomatic adolescent for idiopathic scoliosis because USPSTF supports it.

Use the adult examination with special attention to posture; recognize poor-posture kyphosis and peak sports injuries, and use forward bending when scoliosis is a concern rather than citing USPSTF support for routine asymptomatic screening.
Treat rib humps on forward bending as normal adolescent growth.
Ignore posture because adolescent sports injuries are uncommon.
qs.e: USPSTF does not support routine screening of asymptomatic adolescents for idiopathic scoliosis in this source. When concerned, a rib hump or unequal landmark elevation during forward bending suggests scoliosis.

qs.q: Which pattern is expected during pregnancy?
c: Progressive lordosis; third-trimester anterior cervical flexion, kyphosis, and slumped shoulders; a waddling gait at term.
Progressive loss of lumbar curvature and a narrowing gait at term.
A single C-curve throughout pregnancy with posterior cervical extension as the listed third-trimester change.
A unilateral rib hump is the defining normal pregnancy change.
qs.e: The source describes progressive lordosis during pregnancy. Later changes include anterior cervical flexion, kyphosis, slumped shoulders, and a waddling gait at term.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe aging-adult musculoskeletal assessment?
c: Height loss becomes apparent in the 70s–80s, with lengthening of the arm-trunk axis.
Kyphosis with backward head tilt and slight hip/knee flexion may occur.
Peripheral fat loss with abdominal/hip deposition and prominent bony prominences may occur.
Absent disease, ROM and strength remain much like younger adults; functional ADL assessment is useful with advanced aging, arthritic, or disability changes.
Marked loss of strength and ROM is required for normal aging even without disease.
qs.e: Aging changes posture, height, and fat distribution, but does not by itself require major ROM or strength loss. Functional ADL assessment addresses the effect of advanced aging, arthritis, or disability.

qs.q: For the Get Up and Go Test—rise from an armchair, walk 10 feet, turn, return, and sit—what time or longer indicates increased fall risk?
qs.e: A healthy adult over 60 completes the sequence in under 12 seconds. A result of 12 seconds or more indicates increased fall risk.

qs.q: Which statement correctly identifies the sample charting categories and overall assessment?
c: No pain, stiffness, swelling, weakness, trauma, deformity, activity limits, or occupational MSK risks, plus brisk walking 1 mile 5 times weekly, are subjective; symmetric structures, normal curvature, full smooth ROM without crepitus or tenderness, and maintained flexion against resistance are objective; the assessment is healthy, functional muscles and joints.
Reported daily activities are objective, while observed joint symmetry is subjective.
Exercise frequency is the assessment, and muscle strength is subjective.
The sample describes joint heat, masses, and swelling as healthy objective findings.
qs.e: Subjective information is the person's reported symptoms, history, function, risks, and exercise pattern. Objective findings also include absence of swelling, masses, deformity, heat, and palpation tenderness, supporting the healthy-and-functional assessment.

qs.q: What numeric range should you use for muscle-strength grading in this course?
qs.e: ⚠ Conflict: Slide 37 says “5-point scale,” but her documentation sheet and Jarvis p. 587 specify 0–5. Use 0–5, which contains six grades.

qs.q: Which cervical ROM values and safety rule are correct?
c: Flexion 45°, hyperextension 55°, lateral bending 40°, rotation 70°; do not attempt cervical motions if neck trauma is suspected.
Flexion 75–90°, hyperextension 30°, lateral bending 35°, rotation 30°; always test despite suspected neck trauma.
Flexion 180°, hyperextension 50°, lateral bending 90°, rotation 20°; omit only painful motions after trauma.
Flexion 90°, hyperextension 70°, lateral bending 55°, rotation 45°; suspected trauma is not relevant.
qs.e: The cervical reference values are 45° flexion, 55° hyperextension, 40° lateral bending, and 70° rotation. Suspected neck trauma is a reason not to attempt cervical motions.

qs.q: Which upper-extremity ROM reference set is correct?
c: Shoulder flexion 90° and hyperextension 20°; elbow flexion 70°; pronation/supination 45° each; wrist hyperextension 180° and palmar flexion 50°.
Shoulder flexion 180° and hyperextension up to 50°; elbow flexion 150–160° and pronation/supination 90° each; wrist hyperextension 70° and palmar flexion 90°.
Shoulder flexion 45° and hyperextension 55°; elbow flexion 120°; pronation/supination 30° each; wrist hyperextension 20° and palmar flexion 45°.
Shoulder flexion 130–150° and hyperextension 15°; elbow flexion 35°; pronation/supination 70° each; wrist hyperextension 55° and palmar flexion 40°.
qs.e: These are the Jarvis orientation values for shoulder, elbow, and wrist movements. Her Slide 32 emphasizes bilateral comparison and normally pain-free ROM rather than specifying these numeric ranges.

qs.q: Which lower-extremity ROM reference set is correct?
c: Hip flexion 90° with the leg up or 120° with the knee to chest; knee flexion 130–150° and extension 0° or 15° hyperextension; ankle plantar flexion 45° and dorsiflexion 20°.
Hip flexion 45° or 55°; knee flexion 70° and extension 40°; ankle plantar flexion 90° and dorsiflexion 90°.
Hip flexion 180° or 50°; knee flexion 30° and extension 35°; ankle plantar flexion 20° and dorsiflexion 45°.
Hip flexion 70° or 90°; knee flexion 75–90° and extension 30°; ankle plantar flexion 120° and dorsiflexion 90°.
qs.e: Hip flexion differs with the testing position: 90° with the leg up versus 120° with the knee to chest. The table gives knee extension as 0°, with 15° hyperextension also listed.

qs.q: Which movement definitions are explicitly supported by the supplied motion-pair table?
c: Flexion bends a limb at a joint; extension straightens it.
Abduction moves away from the midline; adduction moves toward it.
Pronation turns the forearm palm down; supination turns it palm up.
Inversion turns the sole of the foot inward.
Abduction moves toward the midline, and pronation turns the palm up.
qs.e: These definitions match the supplied motion table. The chunk ends after the definition of inversion, so it does not supply the definition of eversion.

qs.q: Which bowel-sound procedure should you follow for this instructor?
c: Listen only in the LUQ for 30 seconds before declaring sounds absent.
Start in the RLQ, auscultate all four quadrants, and listen continuously for 5 minutes before declaring sounds absent.
Start in the LLQ and declare sounds absent after 1 minute.
Count sounds for 15 seconds in one quadrant and declare absence if none occur.
qs.e: ⚠ Conflict: Her method requires all four quadrants starting in the RLQ, whereas Jarvis says four-quadrant auscultation is not necessary. Follow her method and listen for 5 minutes continuously before declaring bowel sounds absent.

qs.q: What is the normal bowel-sound frequency range, even though these irregular sounds should not be counted?
qs.e: Normal bowel sounds are irregular and occur approximately 5–30 times per minute. The source specifically says not to count them.

qs.q: Which descriptions and associations of bowel sounds are correct?
c: Hyperactive sounds are loud, high-pitched, rushing, or tinkling and reflect increased motility.
Early obstruction, gastroenteritis, diarrhea, and laxatives are associated with hyperactive sounds.
Surgery, peritonitis, paralytic ileus, and complete obstruction are associated with hypoactive or absent sounds.
Complete obstruction and early obstruction are both listed only under hyperactive sounds.
Hypoactive sounds are defined as loud, high-pitched tinkling caused by increased motility.
qs.e: The source separates increased-motility sounds from hypoactive or absent sounds. Early obstruction is listed with hyperactivity, while complete obstruction is listed with hypoactive or absent sounds.

qs.q: Which comparison of abdominal percussion notes is correct?
c: Tympany is high-pitched and musical over stomach/intestinal air; dullness has medium intensity, duration, and pitch over solid organs, masses, fluid, adipose, or a distended bladder; hyperresonance is very loud, low-pitched, and long with gaseous distention.
Tympany is a medium-pitched sound over fluid; dullness is musical over air; hyperresonance is short and high-pitched.
Tympany identifies only solid organs; dullness identifies only air; hyperresonance indicates a normal spinal curve.
All three notes have identical pitch and duration and cannot be distinguished.
qs.e: Tympany is the musical note associated with air, while dullness is associated with denser contents or structures. Hyperresonance is louder, lower-pitched, and longer in duration and is associated with gaseous distention.

qs.q: Which comparison distinguishes voluntary guarding from involuntary rigidity?
c: Guarding is constant boardlike hardness; rigidity always disappears with exhalation.
Guarding is bilateral and relaxes with exhalation, often with cold, tension, or ticklishness; rigidity is constant boardlike hardness associated with peritoneal inflammation and may be unilateral.
Both findings are always unilateral and caused only by ticklishness.
Rigidity is a normal response to relaxation, while guarding specifically indicates peritoneal inflammation.
qs.e: Relaxation with exhalation favors voluntary guarding. Persistent boardlike hardness favors involuntary rigidity and is associated with peritoneal inflammation.

qs.q: Approximately how deep is light abdominal palpation?
qs.e: Light palpation is approximately 1 cm deep. It is distinguished from deep palpation, which reaches 5–8 cm.

qs.q: What is the depth range for deep abdominal palpation?
qs.e: Deep palpation is 5–8 cm, approximately 2–3 inches. This is deeper than the approximately 1 cm used for light palpation.

qs.q: What is the normal palpable aortic width?
qs.e: The quick-review table lists normal aortic width on palpation as 2.5–4 cm. This value refers to aortic width, not palpation depth.

qs.q: According to the quick-review table, when does the liver-edge finding indicate enlargement?
c: When the edge is more than 1–2 cm below the right costal margin.
Only when the edge is 5–8 cm below the left costal margin.
Whenever normal bowel sounds are irregular.
Only when the aorta measures 2.5–4 cm wide.
qs.e: The table identifies a liver edge more than 1–2 cm below the right costal margin as enlarged. The location and distance both matter.

qs.q: The source states that the spleen becomes palpable only when enlarged to approximately what size?
c: 1.2 times normal.
2 times normal.
3 times normal.
8 times normal.
qs.e: The quick-review table states that the spleen is palpable only when enlarged to three times normal size. Palpability therefore reflects substantial enlargement in this source.

qs.q: What striae length range is listed in lecture?
qs.e: The listed striae length is 1–6 cm. The other abdominal measurements in the table refer to different structures or techniques.

qs.q: The quick-review table warns that shifting dullness may miss fluid below which volume threshold range?
qs.e: The source lists 500–1100 mL as the threshold range below which shifting dullness misses fluid. A negative finding therefore does not establish that no fluid is present.

qs.q: Which statement about an abdominal bruit in healthy people matches the source?
c: It occurs in 4%–20%, usually in people younger than 40, and is usually celiac.
It occurs in every healthy adult older than 80 and is always aortic.
It occurs only with absent bowel sounds.
It is listed as normal in 50%–90% of infants only.
qs.e: The table reports a normal bruit in 4%–20% of healthy people. It is usually celiac and usually occurs in people under age 40.

qs.q: A patient reports no pain during ROM, but only the right side has been examined. Which action fulfills the ROM principle stated on her slide?
c: Compare the corresponding left-side ROM because assessment should be bilateral and normally pain-free.
Stop because absence of pain removes the need for bilateral comparison.
Replace ROM assessment with abdominal percussion.
Assume both sides have identical ROM without examining the left.
qs.e: Slide 32 specifies bilateral comparison and normally pain-free ROM. Assessing only one side leaves the comparison incomplete.

qs.q: Which clinical interpretations correctly apply the special-test findings?
c: Numbness and burning reproduced by Phalen testing support carpal tunnel syndrome.
A visible fluid wave during the bulge sign indicates a small knee effusion, while patellar ballottement detects larger fluid amounts.
A click during McMurray testing suggests a torn meniscus and orthopedic referral.
The opposite thigh lifting during the Thomas test indicates hip flexion deformity.
Sciatic pain worsened by dorsiflexion during straight leg raising is the positive finding for carpal tunnel syndrome.
qs.e: Special tests must be linked to their specific positive findings rather than treated interchangeably. Sciatic pain worsened during straight leg raising is associated with a herniated disc, not carpal tunnel syndrome.

qs.q: An older adult has kyphosis with backward head tilt. Which additional finding would match the source's aging pattern rather than automatically imply disease-related loss of function?
c: Slight hip and knee flexion with ROM and strength much like those of younger adults.
Mandatory severe weakness despite absence of disease.
A requirement that all spinal curves disappear.
A normal Get Up and Go result defined as 12 seconds or longer.
qs.e: Postural changes can coexist with relatively preserved ROM and strength in aging adults without disease. A Get Up and Go result of 12 seconds or longer instead indicates increased fall risk.

qs.q: A child older than 3 years continues to show pronation and lacks a foot arch. How should this be interpreted using the source?
c: As abnormal persistence beyond the stated age for expected resolution.
As normal at every age because infant pes planus is normal.
As a positive Allis test.
As the expected definition of adolescent kyphosis.
qs.e: Pes planus is normal in infants and resolves by age 3 in lecture. Pronation or lack of an arch after age 3 is identified as abnormal.

qs.q: A patient's apparent leg lengths differ, but true lengths are equal. Which explanation is supported by the source?
c: Pelvic obliquity or hip adduction/flexion deformity.
Carpal tunnel syndrome.
Normal infant cervical-curve development.
A small knee effusion proven by the length measurements alone.
qs.e: Apparent leg length can be unequal despite equal true lengths with pelvic obliquity or hip adduction/flexion deformity. True and apparent measurements use different starting landmarks.

qs.q: Which pair correctly defines flexion and extension?
c: Flexion bends a limb at a joint; extension straightens it.
Flexion straightens a limb at a joint; extension bends it.
Flexion moves a limb away from the midline; extension moves it toward the midline.
Flexion turns the palm down; extension turns it up.
qs.e: Flexion is bending a limb at a joint. Extension is the opposite movement: straightening the limb at the joint.

qs.q: A client moves an arm away from the midline and then returns it toward the midline. Which movements occurred, in order?
c: Adduction, then abduction
Abduction, then adduction
Flexion, then extension
Pronation, then supination
qs.e: Abduction moves a body part away from the midline. Adduction moves it toward the midline.

qs.q: Which description correctly distinguishes pronation from supination?
c: Pronation turns the sole inward; supination turns it outward.
Pronation turns the palm up; supination turns it down.
Pronation turns the forearm palm down; supination turns it palm up.
Pronation bends a joint; supination straightens it.
qs.e: Pronation turns the forearm so the palm faces down. Supination turns the palm up.

qs.q: Which movement pair occurs at the ankle?
c: Inversion turns the sole outward; eversion turns it inward.
Inversion turns the palm down; eversion turns it up.
Inversion straightens the limb; eversion bends it.
Inversion turns the sole inward; eversion turns it outward.
qs.e: Inversion turns the sole of the foot inward at the ankle. Eversion turns the sole outward.

qs.q: Which examples correctly identify circumduction or rotation? Select all that apply.
c: Moving the arm in circles around the shoulder is circumduction.
Turning the head around its central axis is rotation.
Turning the palm down is circumduction.
Moving a limb toward the midline is rotation.
Turning the sole outward is circumduction.
qs.e: Circumduction is illustrated by arm circles around the shoulder. Rotation is illustrated by turning the head around its central axis.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe active and passive range-of-motion assessment? Select all that apply.
c: Assess active motion first, with the client moving voluntarily while you model the motion.
Use passive motion only if active motion is limited.
During passive motion, you move the part while the client's muscles are relaxed.
Normally, active and passive motion ranges should be the same.
Begin with passive motion for every joint.
qs.e: Active ROM is always assessed first. Passive ROM is used only when active motion is limited, and normal active and passive ranges should match.

qs.q: Which pairing correctly distinguishes muscle strength grades 5 and 4?
c: 5 = full ROM with some resistance, Good; 4 = full ROM with gravity alone, Fair.
5 = full ROM against gravity and full resistance, Normal; 4 = full ROM against gravity and some resistance, Good.
5 = slight contraction, Trace; 4 = no contraction, Zero.
5 = full ROM with gravity eliminated, Poor; 4 = full ROM against gravity and full resistance, Normal.
qs.e: Per the source, muscle strength is graded 0–5 (six grades). Grade 5 is Normal: full ROM against gravity with full resistance. Grade 4 is Good: full ROM against gravity with some resistance.
qs.src: [Slide 37; Study guide; Doc sheet; Jarvis p. 587]

qs.q: Which pairing correctly distinguishes muscle strength grades 3 and 2?
c: 3 = full ROM with gravity, Fair; 2 = full ROM with gravity eliminated, Poor.
3 = full ROM against full resistance, Normal; 2 = full ROM against some resistance, Good.
3 = slight contraction, Trace; 2 = no contraction, Zero.
3 = full ROM with gravity eliminated, Poor; 2 = full ROM with gravity, Fair.
qs.e: Per the source, muscle strength is graded 0–5 (six grades). Grade 3 is Fair: full ROM with gravity. Grade 2 is Poor: full ROM only when gravity is eliminated.
qs.src: [Slide 37; Study guide; Doc sheet; Jarvis p. 587]

qs.q: Which pairing correctly distinguishes muscle strength grades 1 and 0?
c: 1 = full ROM with gravity eliminated, Poor; 0 = slight contraction, Trace.
1 = no contraction, Zero; 0 = slight contraction, Trace.
1 = slight contraction, Trace; 0 = no contraction, Zero.
1 = full ROM with gravity, Fair; 0 = full ROM with gravity eliminated, Poor.
qs.e: Per the source, muscle strength is graded 0–5 (six grades). Grade 1 is Trace: a slight contraction. Grade 0 is Zero: no contraction.
qs.src: [Slide 37; Study guide; Doc sheet; Jarvis p. 587]

qs.q: Which abdominal examination sequence is correct, and why?
c: Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation, because palpation preserves bowel sounds.
Auscultation, inspection, palpation, percussion, because inspection alters peristalsis.
Inspection, percussion, auscultation, palpation, because percussion must precede listening.
Inspection, auscultation, percussion, palpation, because percussion and palpation can alter peristalsis.
qs.e: Inspect first, auscultate second, then percuss and palpate. Listening before percussion and palpation avoids changes in peristalsis caused by those maneuvers.

qs.q: Using the instructor's bowel-sound method, which actions are correct? Select all that apply.
c: Start in the right lower quadrant.
Use the diaphragm of the stethoscope.
Auscultate all four quadrants.
Listen continuously for 5 minutes before declaring sounds absent.
Declare sounds absent after listening only briefly over the ileocecal valve area.
qs.e: Per the instructor's method: start in the RLQ (ileocecal valve area) with the diaphragm, auscultate all four quadrants beginning there, and listen continuously for 5 minutes before declaring bowel sounds absent.

qs.q: Before declaring bowel sounds absent, how long must continuous auscultation last?
qs.e: Absent bowel sounds require 5 minutes of continuous auscultation. Brief silence is not enough to declare absence.

qs.q: Which conditions or exposures are associated with hyperactive bowel sounds and increased motility? Select all that apply.
c: Early obstruction
Gastroenteritis or diarrhea
Laxatives
Subsiding paralytic ileus
Complete obstruction
qs.e: Hyperactive sounds indicate increased motility and occur with early obstruction, gastroenteritis, diarrhea, laxatives, and subsiding paralytic ileus. Complete obstruction belongs with hypoactive or absent sounds.

qs.q: Which situations are associated with hypoactive or absent bowel sounds? Select all that apply.
c: Surgery
Peritonitis
Paralytic ileus
Complete obstruction
Laxative use
qs.e: The source associates surgery, peritonitis, paralytic ileus, and complete obstruction with hypoactive or absent bowel sounds. Laxatives are associated with hyperactive sounds.

qs.q: Which description correctly defines a bruit and its associated mechanisms?
c: A high-pitched musical percussion note caused by intestinal air
A pulsatile blowing vascular sound, usually systolic and medium-to-low pitched, associated with stenosis, partial occlusion, or aneurysm
An irregular gurgling sound caused by movement of intestinal air and fluid
An audible crunch caused by roughened articular surfaces
qs.e: A bruit is a pulsatile blowing sound heard over an artery, usually systolic and medium-to-low pitched. It may occur with stenosis, partial occlusion, or an aneurysm.

qs.q: Over which vessels should you auscultate for abdominal bruits? Select all that apply.
c: Aorta
Renal arteries
Iliac arteries
Femoral arteries
Ileocecal valve
qs.e: The specified bruit sites are the aorta and renal, iliac, and femoral arteries. The ileocecal valve area is the starting location for bowel sounds, not an artery.

qs.q: Which statements match the source's recommendations for percussion? Select all that apply.
c: Do not use percussion to determine liver span.
Do not use percussion to determine splenomegaly.
Do not use percussion to determine bladder distention.
Percuss the costovertebral angle to assess kidney tenderness.
Use percussion rather than palpation as the preferred way to detect splenomegaly.
qs.e: Percussion is not recommended here for determining liver span, splenomegaly, or bladder distention. Costovertebral-angle percussion is used to assess kidney tenderness.

qs.q: Which interpretation of abdominal percussion findings is correct?
c: Dullness normally predominates because air rises when supine.
Hyperresonance indicates solid organs, while tympany indicates fluid.
Tympany normally predominates as air rises when supine; dullness occurs over solid organs, masses, fluid, adipose, or a distended bladder; hyperresonance indicates gaseous distention.
Tympany indicates splenomegaly, while dullness indicates gaseous distention.
qs.e: Tympany predominates normally because of abdominal air, which rises in the supine position. Dullness occurs over denser contents, while hyperresonance indicates gaseous distention.

qs.q: Which combination correctly describes abdominal palpation depth and technique?
c: Light: approximately 1 cm; deep: approximately 5–8 cm; bimanual technique for a very large or obese abdomen
Light: approximately 5–8 cm; deep: approximately 1 cm; bimanual technique only for thin people
Light: approximately 1 cm; deep: approximately 1–2 cm; avoid bimanual technique in obesity
Light: approximately 5 cm; deep: approximately 8–10 cm; bimanual technique replaces all light palpation
qs.e: Light palpation is approximately 1 cm deep, and deep palpation is approximately 5–8 cm. A bimanual technique is used for a very large or obese abdomen.

qs.q: What is the purpose of light abdominal palpation?
c: To determine liver span
To find all abdominal organs
To elicit a fluid wave
To form an overall impression of the skin surface and superficial musculature
qs.e: Light palpation provides an overall impression of the skin surface and superficial musculature. Its purpose is not to locate organs.

qs.q: Which actions are appropriate when assessing an abdomen with tenderness? Select all that apply.
c: Assess tender areas last.
Watch for nonverbal cues of discomfort.
Assess tender areas first.
Ignore nonverbal cues if the client does not report pain.
Begin rebound testing by pressing directly into the tender area.
qs.e: Tender areas should be assessed last, and nonverbal discomfort cues should be observed. The described rebound technique starts in a non-tender area.

qs.q: Which statement correctly classifies abdominal contours?
c: Scaphoid and protuberant are normal; flat and rounded are abnormal.
Only a scaphoid contour is normal.
Flat to rounded is normal; scaphoid means caved in and protuberant means distended, both abnormal.
Rounded means caved in, and scaphoid means distended.
qs.e: Normal abdominal contour ranges from flat to rounded. A scaphoid abdomen caves inward, while a protuberant abdomen is distended; both are classified as abnormal in this source.

qs.q: Which umbilical finding and interpretation are correct?
c: Normally midline and inverted; eversion may occur with ascites or an umbilical hernia.
Normally lateral and inverted; a midline position indicates ascites.
Normally midline and everted; inversion indicates hernia.
Normally lateral and everted; inversion indicates peritonitis.
qs.e: The umbilicus is normally midline and inverted. An everted umbilicus is associated with ascites or an umbilical hernia.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe striae? Select all that apply.
c: They are a common abdominal pigment change.
They may be silvery-white, linear, jagged marks 1–6 cm long.
They result from broken elastic fibers after stretching, such as pregnancy or weight gain.
Recent striae may be pink or blue.
They are pulsatile vascular sounds caused by partial arterial occlusion.
qs.e: Striae are common skin changes caused by broken elastic fibers after stretching. They are often silvery-white, linear, jagged, and 1–6 cm long, but recent marks may be pink or blue.

qs.q: What is the upper central abdominal region just below the xiphoid in the nine-region scheme?
qs.e: The epigastrium is the upper central region just below the xiphoid. Visible aortic pulsation here can be normal in thin, relaxed people.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes splenomegaly and the safety response to palpating an enlarged spleen?
c: The spleen is normally palpable; continue deep palpation if it feels enlarged.
Splenomegaly means liver enlargement and is best detected by percussion.
The spleen becomes palpable at half its normal size; repeat palpation to confirm.
Splenomegaly means an enlarged spleen; it is normally not palpable, must be about three times normal size to be felt, and palpation should stop if enlargement is felt.
qs.e: Splenomegaly is best detected by palpation rather than percussion; the spleen normally is not palpable and must be about three times normal size to be felt. Jarvis p. 552 adds a caution not in the slides: stop palpating an enlarged spleen because it is friable and can rupture.

qs.q: Which finding matches the source's description of an abdominal aortic aneurysm?
c: A caved-in contour without pulsation
Abnormal arterial widening with a widened aortic pulsation (>2.5–4 cm), prominent lateral pulsation, and a possible systolic bruit
An inverted umbilicus with normal bowel sounds
A discrete joint crack caused by a tendon slipping over bone
qs.e: An aneurysm is abnormal widening or dilation of an artery. The listed abdominal aortic findings include a widened pulsation (>2.5–4 cm), prominent lateral pulsation, and possibly a systolic bruit.

qs.q: Which findings or definitions are associated with ascites? Select all that apply.
c: Free fluid in the peritoneal cavity
An everted umbilicus and bulging flanks
Taut, glistening skin with tympany over the top and dullness over fluid
A positive fluid wave and shifting dullness
A scaphoid abdomen caused by an inward-caving contour
qs.e: Ascites is free fluid in the peritoneal cavity. The source lists an everted umbilicus, bulging flanks, taut glistening skin, tympany above fluid, dullness over fluid, a positive fluid wave, and shifting dullness.

qs.q: What term means loud hyperperistalsis heard as hyperactive 'stomach growling'?
qs.e: Borborygmi are loud hyperperistalsis. They are heard as hyperactive bowel sounds or 'stomach growling.'

qs.q: What is the normal bowel-sound frequency per minute?
qs.e: Normal bowel sounds are high-pitched, gurgling, cascading, irregular sounds occurring 5–30 times per minute, produced by movement of air and fluid in the stomach and small and large intestines. The source uses the assessment categories Present, Hyperactive, and Hypoactive.

qs.q: Which finding fits the source's definition of hepatomegaly?
c: A liver edge more than 1–2 cm below the right costal margin, except with a depressed diaphragm
A spleen approximately three times its normal size
Free fluid in the peritoneal cavity
A liver edge associated only with a normal discrete joint crack
qs.e: Hepatomegaly means abnormal enlargement of the liver. The source describes a liver edge palpated more than 1–2 cm below the right costal margin, with an exception for a depressed diaphragm.

qs.q: What high-pitched, musical percussion note is produced by air in the stomach and intestines?
qs.e: Tympany is produced by air in the stomach and intestines. It normally predominates over the abdomen.

qs.q: Which approach correctly describes the joint examination?
c: Palpate before inspecting; joint tenderness is normal.
Inspect only; temperature and the joint capsule are not assessed.
Inspect, then palpate temperature, muscles, bony articulations, and the joint capsule; joints should be non-tender.
Assess only motion; omit inspection and palpation.
qs.e: The joint examination begins with inspection, followed by palpation of temperature, muscles, bony articulations, and the joint capsule. Normal joints are non-tender.

qs.q: What is range of motion, and what findings are normal?
c: The strength of a muscle contraction; normal findings include unequal motion and pain.
The arc of movement of a joint; compare bilaterally and expect equal motion without tenderness, pain, or crepitation.
The inward curve of the lumbar spine; compare only passive motion.
The sound of a tendon slipping over bone; tenderness is expected.
qs.e: Range of motion is the arc of movement of a joint. Compare sides and expect equal bilateral motion without tenderness, pain, or crepitation.

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes crepitation from a normal joint sound?
c: Crepitation is a normal discrete crack from a tendon slipping over bone.
All joint sounds indicate roughened articular surfaces.
A discrete tendon-over-bone crack is the same as abnormal grating.
Crepitation is abnormal audible and palpable crunching or grating from roughened articular surfaces, as in RA; a discrete tendon-over-bone crack can be normal.
qs.e: Crepitation is abnormal crunching or grating accompanying movement when articular surfaces are roughened, such as in RA. It differs from the normal discrete crack of a tendon slipping over bone.

qs.q: Which finding represents normal muscle strength?
c: Equal strength bilaterally, fully resisting opposing force, with grade 5 representing full ROM against gravity and full resistance
Unequal strength bilaterally with full ROM only when gravity is eliminated
Equal strength bilaterally with only a slight contraction
No contraction despite an attempt to move
qs.e: Per the source, muscle strength is graded 0–5 (six grades). Normal strength is equal bilaterally and fully resists opposing force; grade 5 requires full ROM against gravity and full resistance.
qs.src: [Slide 37; Study guide; Doc sheet; Jarvis p. 587]

qs.q: What term describes an enhanced outward thoracic spinal curve, common with aging and adolescent poor posture?
qs.e: Kyphosis is an enhanced outward curve of the thoracic spine. The source associates it with aging and adolescent poor posture.

qs.q: What term describes a pronounced inward lumbar spinal curve, common with obesity, pregnancy, and childhood?
qs.e: Lordosis is a pronounced inward curve of the lumbar spine. It is associated here with obesity, pregnancy, and childhood.

qs.q: What vocabulary term means muscle pain or aching?
qs.e: Myalgias are muscle pain or aching and are assessed in the musculoskeletal history. Reporting no muscle pain or weakness is a normal response.

qs.q: Which description identifies scoliosis?
c: An enhanced outward thoracic curve associated with aging
A pronounced inward lumbar curve associated with pregnancy
Lateral spinal curvature with unequal shoulder, scapula, or iliac crest levels and a rib hump on the forward-bend test
Muscle aching without a spinal curve change
qs.e: Scoliosis is lateral curvature of the spine. Findings include unequal shoulder, scapula, or iliac crest levels and a rib hump during the forward-bend test.

qs.q: Which visible abdominal finding can be normal in a thin, relaxed person?
c: Aortic pulsation in the epigastrium
An everted umbilicus with bulging flanks
A scaphoid contour
A protuberant contour indicating distention
qs.e: Visible epigastric aortic pulsation can be normal in thin, relaxed people. This should not be confused with the widened, prominent lateral pulsation described for an abdominal aortic aneurysm.

cards.def: Good lighting; relaxed, comfortable client; have client empty bladder; supine position with arms at sides or across chest and knees bent or on pillow; drape client appropriately; ask regarding presence of tenderness; warm hands and stethoscope; short fingernails.
The abdomen is divided into four quadrants used to identify underlying abdominal organs in relation to landmarks.
An alternative anatomical division of the abdomen into nine regions for organ localization.
Determine profile from rib margin to pubic bone. Contour describes nutritional state and normally ranges from flat to rounded.
Abdomen should be symmetric bilaterally. Note any localized bulging, visible mass, or asymmetric shape. Asking the client to take a deep breath may make masses and enlarged organs more visible.
Normally midline and inverted, with no sign of discoloration, inflammation, or hernia.

Surface smooth and even with homogeneous color. Pigmented nevi (moles) are common. Lesions and rashes are not normally present. Surgical scars may be present—assess cause and document location and length. Fine venous network may be visible in thin persons.
One common pigment change seen on abdominal skin; stretch marks visible on inspection.

Normally, pulsations from the aorta may be seen beneath skin in the epigastric area, particularly in thin persons with good muscle wall relaxation. Respiratory movement also shows in the abdomen, particularly in males. Waves of peristalsis are sometimes visible in very thin persons.
Auscultate with the diaphragm of the stethoscope, noting character and frequency of bowel sounds, beginning in the RLQ (right lower quadrant).
High-pitched, gurgling, and cascading in nature.
Loud, high-pitched, rushing, tinkling sounds due to increased motility associated with early obstruction, gastroenteritis, diarrhea, laxatives, or subsiding paralytic ileus.
Due to abdominal surgery, peritonitis, paralytic ileus, or complete obstruction. Establish absence only after 5 minutes of continuous auscultation to all 4 quadrants.
Auscultate for vascular sounds or bruits over the abdominal aorta, renal, iliac, and femoral arteries.
Percuss to assess relative density of abdominal contents, to locate organs, and to screen for abnormal fluid or masses.
High-pitched, musical percussion sound; indicates presence of air in the stomach and intestine.
Medium intensity, duration, and pitch percussion sound; found over solid organs, masses, fluid, adipose tissue, and distended bladder.
Very loud intensity, low pitch, long duration percussion sound; indicates gaseous distention.
Percussion of the costovertebral angle for kidney tenderness. Percussion is not recommended for determining liver span, splenomegaly, or bladder distention.
Performed to assess size, location, and consistency of certain organs and to screen for an abnormal mass or tenderness. Assess tender areas last and observe for non-verbal cues of discomfort.

Depress abdominal wall approximately 1 cm. Objective is to form an overall impression of skin surface and superficial musculature. Note increased resistance, muscle guarding, and tenderness (normally abdomen is soft and smooth).

Depress abdominal wall approximately 5–8 cm. Used to delineate organs and masses; note location, size, consistency, and mobility of any palpable organs and presence of abnormal enlargement, tenderness, or masses.
A deep palpation method used for very large or obese patients, with one hand on each side of the abdomen.

Determines the presence of peritoneal irritation or inflammation. Slowly and deeply press into the abdomen at a 90-degree angle at a non-tender area, then quickly withdraw fingers. Normally no pain occurs when fingers are withdrawn.
Abdominal distention, abdominal pain, hernia, abnormal bowel sounds, and enlarged organs are key abnormal findings requiring appropriate nursing actions.
Assessment of joints, muscles, and bones, including functional assessment of activities of daily living (ADLs).
Bones united by interjacent fibrous tissue or cartilage that do not move (e.g., sutures in the skull).
Separated by fibrous cartilage and are slightly moveable (e.g., vertebrae).
Freely moveable joints separated from one another and enclosed in a cavity lined with synovial membrane that secretes fluid.
Note size and contour of joints. Inspect skin and tissue overlying joints for color, swelling, masses, or deformity.
Palpate each joint for skin temperature, muscles, bony articulations, and joint capsule. Joints are normally non-tender when palpated.
Have the client move through active ROM; if limitation occurs, move joint through passive ROM. Compare joints bilaterally. Normally no tenderness, pain, or crepitation is present.
Bending a limb at a joint.
Straightening a limb at a joint.
Moving a limb away from the midline of the body.
Moving a limb toward the midline of the body.
Turning the forearm so that the palm is down.
Turning the forearm so that the palm is up.
Moving the arm in a circle around the shoulder.
Moving the sole of the foot inward at the ankle.
Moving the sole of the foot outward at the ankle.
Moving the head around a central axis.
An instrument used to measure the angle of a joint during range of motion assessment.
Perform abdominal assessment through inspection, auscultation, percussion, and palpation — in that order every time.
Normally midline and inverted with no discoloration, inflammation, or hernia.
Auscultate with diaphragm for character and frequency; normal sounds are high-pitched, gurgling, cascading. Document as present, hyperactive, or hypoactive.

⚠ Conflict: Instructor method (follow this on the exam) — begin in the RLQ and auscultate all four quadrants; absence of bowel sounds is established only after 5 minutes of continuous auscultation to all 4 quadrants [Slide 17]. Jarvis says sounds radiate widely, so listening in all four quadrants is not necessary (just judge present / hypoactive / hyperactive), but agrees on the 5-minute rule for absence [Jarvis p. 545]. Her rule is stricter; follow her.
Diminished or absent sounds; may occur with surgery, peritonitis, paralytic ileus, or complete obstruction.
Vascular sound heard on auscultation; auscultate the aorta, renal, iliac, and femoral arteries for bruits.
Upper central region of the abdomen; aortic pulsation may be visible here in thin persons.
Abnormal protrusion through a body wall; normally the umbilicus has no hernia. Hernia is one of the abnormal abdominal findings to recognize.
Abnormal dilation of a blood vessel such as the aorta; may present as abnormal pulsations visible on inspection or bruits on auscultation of aortic, renal, iliac, or femoral arteries.
Fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity causing abdominal distention; contributes to abnormal contour findings on inspection.
Loud, gurgling bowel sounds heard on auscultation; associated with hyperactive or increased bowel sounds and increased motility.
Enlargement of the liver; may be revealed on deep breath or deep palpation as an enlarged organ or mass.
Enlargement of the spleen; classified under abnormal findings of enlarged organs on abdominal assessment.
Three types: fibrous (no movement, e.g., skull sutures), cartilaginous (slightly moveable, e.g., vertebrae), and synovial (freely moveable, synovial membrane secretes fluid).
Assess size and contour; skin/tissue color, swelling, masses, and deformity. Compare bilaterally.
Assess skin temperature, muscles, bony articulations, and joint capsule. Joints are normally non-tender; note tenderness and swelling.
Assess ROM in this order: TMJ, cervical spine, shoulder, elbow, wrist & hand, hip, knee, ankle & foot, spine.

⚠ Conflict: Her slide says grade on a "5-point scale" [Slide 37]; the actual Muscle Grading Scale is 0–5 (six grades) [Jarvis p. 587], and her own documentation sheet says "numeric value from 0–5 … Muscle Grading Scale p. 587" [Module page]. Use the 0–5 scale. Assess strength of muscles surrounding each joint through the same motions as for AROM; strength should be equal bilaterally and fully resist opposing force. Document numeric 0–5 for deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist, fingers, hips, quads, hamstrings, ankles/feet.
Grating, crackling, or popping sensation with joint movement; normally absent during ROM assessment.
Excessive outward curvature of the thoracic spine (hunchback); a musculoskeletal vocab term for spinal deformity.
Excessive inward curvature of the lumbar spine (swayback); a musculoskeletal vocab term for spinal deformity.
Lateral curvature of the spine; a musculoskeletal vocab term for spinal deformity.
Muscle pain or aches; a musculoskeletal symptom to note during assessment.
Documentation abbreviation used in the Module 4 documentation sheet to indicate a finding is within normal defined limits. Key: ✔ = WNDL, X = abnormal, Ø = absent.
The abdomen is divided into four quadrants (RUQ, RLQ, LUQ, LLQ) by horizontal and vertical midlines; used to locate organs and describe findings.
An alternative anatomical division of the abdomen into nine regions; diagram referenced on Slide 8 (Seidel/Mosby).
Right upper quadrant contains the liver (edge and lower border), gallbladder (under liver border), right kidney lower pole, and ascending colon.
Right lower quadrant contains the cecum, ileocecal valve area (bowel sounds always present here), and appendix region (McBurney point).
Left upper quadrant contains the spleen (not normally palpable) and left kidney (about 1 cm higher than right, not normally palpable).
Left lower quadrant contains the sigmoid colon; mild tenderness is normally present here.

Key landmarks include the xiphoid process, rectus muscles (lateral borders), sacral promontory, pulsatile aorta (upper abdomen slightly left of midline), and full bladder/gravid uterus (lower midline).
Determined from rib margin to pubic bone; normally flat to rounded, describing nutritional state. Charting options: flat, rounded, scaphoid, or protuberant.
The abdomen caves in (concave profile), indicating a scaphoid contour.
The abdomen is distended or bulging outward, indicating a protuberant contour.

The abdomen should be symmetric bilaterally; note localized bulging, visible mass, or asymmetric shape. Shine a light across the abdomen to highlight bulges; ask client to take a deep breath or sit up to reveal masses.
Normally midline and inverted, with no discoloration, inflammation, or hernia. Everted with ascites or mass; deeply sunken with obesity; enlarged/everted with umbilical hernia.
A hard umbilical nodule associated with metastatic cancer of the stomach, large intestine, ovary, or pancreas.
Bluish periumbilical discoloration (rare), indicating intraperitoneal bleeding.
Prominent dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus, indicating portal hypertension, cirrhosis, ascites, or vena caval obstruction.
Pinch a skin fold and release; poor turgor indicates dehydration, common with GI disease.
Normally a diamond pattern in adult males and an inverted triangle in adult females.

Normal is relaxed with benign expression and slow even respirations. Restlessness suggests colicky pain; absolute stillness resisting movement suggests peritonitis; knees flexed with facial grimacing and rapid uneven respirations indicate pain.

Per instructor (lab check-off): auscultate all four quadrants with the diaphragm, starting in the RLQ at the ileocecal valve area (bowel sounds always present here). Do not declare sounds absent until you have auscultated continuously for a full 5 minutes. ⚠ Conflict: Her slide [Slide 17] says to auscultate "to 4 quadrants"; Jarvis states listening in all four quadrants is NOT necessary because bowel sounds radiate widely [Jarvis p. 545] — just judge present / hypoactive / hyperactive. Use the instructor's 4-quadrant method for lab check-off. Both sources agree on the 5-minute rule before declaring sounds absent.
Hyperperistalsis or 'stomach growling'; a fairly common type of hyperactive bowel sound.

Assesses relative density of abdominal contents, locates organs, and screens for abnormal fluid or masses. Percuss lightly in all four quadrants moving clockwise; tympany should predominate when supine.

Costovertebral angle percussion for kidney tenderness: place one hand over the 12th rib at the CVA and thump with the ulnar edge of the other fist. Normal is a thud with no pain; sharp pain suggests kidney or perinephric inflammation (e.g., pyelonephritis).

An advanced ascites percussion test: a firm hand in midline blocks skin transmission while the opposite flank is struck; a positive result is a distinct tap felt on the far side, indicating large ascites.

An ascites percussion test: percuss from tympany over the top down to dullness at the flank fluid level while supine, mark it, roll the person to the right side, and repeat; the level of dullness shifts upward. Positive only with large volumes (>500-1100 mL).
Increased resistance or tensing of the abdominal musculature in response to touch, often due to pain or inflammation; examine painful areas last to avoid guarding.
Protrusion of abdominal viscera through an abnormal opening in the muscle wall; may appear as a bulge with deep breath or sit-up.
With ascites the skin appears glistening and taut, the umbilicus is everted, striae may occur, and prominent dilated veins (caput medusae) may be present.
