Techniques to relax the client during palpation include slow breathing, emotive imagery, low soothing voice, conversation, or having the person relate abdominal history while you palpate.
Not recommended — percussion underestimates true liver size and often misses hepatomegaly; assess the liver by palpation instead.

Normally aortic pulsations may be visible beneath the skin in the epigastric area, especially in thin persons. Marked aortic pulsation with widened pulse pressure suggests hypertension, aortic insufficiency, thyrotoxicosis, or aortic aneurysm.
Assess size, location, consistency of organs; screen for abnormal mass or tenderness. Assess tender areas last and observe non-verbal cues of discomfort.
Bilateral, relaxes slightly on exhalation; caused by cold, tense, or ticklish patient. Use relaxation measures (bend knees, slow breathing, low voice).
Constant, boardlike hardness; may be unilateral; protective response with acute peritoneal inflammation. The same area hurts when the person attempts a sit-up.

Left hand under the back at 11th–12th ribs lifts/supports; right hand on RUQ, fingers parallel to midline, push deeply under right costal margin; with each exhalation move up 1–2 cm. Normal = firm regular ridge bumping fingertips on inhalation, or not palpable at all.
Liver >1–2 cm below right costal margin = enlarged (except with depressed diaphragm). Record cm, consistency, and tenderness. Chronic emphysema displaces liver downward but size is normal.
Hook fingers over costal margin from above while person takes a deep breath; alternative liver palpation method.
Stethoscope at xiphoid, stroke finger up midclavicular line from RLQ; sound magnified at liver edge. Useful when abdomen is distended, obese, too tender, or guarded.

Normally not palpable—must be enlarged 3× normal size to be felt. Left hand behind left side at 11th–12th ribs lifts; right hand oblique on LUQ toward left axilla, push under left costal margin, deep breath. Alternative: roll person onto right side.

If enlarged spleen is felt, stop palpating and refer (friable, ruptures easily); describe cm below costal margin. Enlarged with mononucleosis, trauma, leukemia/lymphomas, portal hypertension, HIV; consider malaria with fever + travel.
'Duck-bill' hands at flank, firm pressure, deep breath—right kidney occasionally felt as round smooth mass sliding between fingers (normal); left kidney sits 1 cm higher and is not normally palpable.
Opposing thumb and fingers, upper abdomen slightly left of midline; normally 2.5–4 cm wide, pulsating anteriorly. Widened/lateral pulsation pushing fingers apart = abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Widened aorta (>2.5–4 cm) with lateral pulsation pushing fingers apart. Palpation accuracy is poor due to skin/adipose tissue and retroperitoneal position.
Fingers under liver border, patient takes deep breath. Positive = sharp pain and abrupt stop of inspiration midway = cholecystitis. Less accurate in patients >60 y (25% have no abdominal tenderness).
Point 1.5–2 inches from the anterior superior iliac spine along the line to the umbilicus; maximal tenderness here with appendicitis.
Supine, lift right leg straight up flexing at hip, push down on distal thigh as person resists. Positive = RLQ pain (inflamed/perforated appendix).
Right leg flexed 90° at hip and knee, rotate internally/externally. Positive = pain (inflamed appendix irritating obturator muscle); less specific.

Migration to right iliac fossa 1, Anorexia 1, Nausea/vomiting 1, Tenderness RLQ 2, Rebound 1, Elevation of temperature (oral ≥37.3°C) 1, Leukocytosis (WBC >10,000/µL) 2, Shift to left (>75% neutrophils) 1—total 10. Score ≤4 decreases probability of appendicitis; ≥7 increases it.
RLQ rebound tenderness with LLQ pressure; may indicate appendicitis. Refer for CT.
Abnormal finding from multiple causes (obesity, air/gas, ascites, ovarian cyst, pregnancy, feces, tumor). Each cause has characteristic inspection and percussion/palpation findings.
Palpable wave of fluid transmitted across abdomen; present with ascites and large ovarian cyst but not with obesity or gas.
Associated with abdominal surgery, peritonitis, paralytic ileus, complete obstruction. Assess all 4 quadrants starting in RLQ; listen 5 minutes before concluding bowel sounds are absent.
Auscultate all 4 quadrants starting in RLQ; listen 5 minutes before declaring bowel sounds absent.

History of prior abdominal surgery with adhesions; vomiting, fever, absence of stool/gas, colicky pain. Exam: distended abdomen; hyperactive sounds early → hypoactive/silent late; possible hypovolemic shock (increased pulse, decreased BP, cool skin, dry mucous membranes).
Midline bulge from separated rectus muscles; more common with Black infants; refer if lasting >6 years.
Appears at 2–3 weeks, most prominent with crying, max at 1 month (up to 2.5 cm/1 in), usually gone by 1 year. Refer if >2.5 cm; asymptomatic hernias monitored to 4–5 years.
First stool = greenish-black meconium within 24 h; by day 4 breastfed = golden yellow, pasty, sour-milk smell; formula-fed = brown-yellow, firmer, fecal smelling.
Inflammation of the peritoneal lining causing involuntary rigidity (boardlike), rebound tenderness, and localized cough tenderness; e.g., from appendicitis or perforation.

5-point scale grading muscle strength: 0 = no contraction; 1 = flicker/trace contraction; 2 = active movement with gravity eliminated; 3 = active movement against gravity; 4 = active movement against gravity and some resistance; 5 = normal full strength against resistance.

Bend knees; keep palpating hand low and parallel to abdomen; slow breathing (in nose, out mouth); low soothing voice; emotive imagery. For ticklish people, place their hand under yours or palpate with stethoscope right after auscultation.
Abnormal finding requiring assessment of location, onset, character, duration, and aggravating/relieving factors; combined with palpation and special tests to determine cause.
Abnormal finding including hyperactive (increased motility), hypoactive (decreased motility), or absent (no motility); assessed by auscultation in all 4 quadrants.
Abnormal finding detectable by palpation: liver >1–2 cm below costal margin, palpable spleen (3× normal size), widened aorta (aneurysm).
Rigid abdominal wall on palpation associated with acute abdomen; less common in aging patients, who often complain of less pain than younger patients.
Abdomen is distended with everted umbilicus and bulging flanks; tympany at dome of abdomen, dullness over flanks. Documented as objective Jarvis charting language.
Visible dilated veins across the abdomen; an abnormal inspection finding noted on the distended abdomen (caput medusae pattern).
Tympany is the drum-like resonance normally present over the dome of the abdomen; dullness over the flanks suggests fluid accumulation. Use overall percussion sound as documented on the exam sheet.
Palpable wave of fluid transmitted across the abdomen when one flank is tapped and the opposite hand feels the impulse; indicates ascites.
Abnormal liver palpation finding documented in objective charting; suggests cirrhosis or chronic liver disease (compare with smooth, nontender normal liver).
Palpation technique to assess for smooth, soft, rigid, guarding, and tenderness; documented on the exam sheet (Jarvis p. 548).
Note contour, symmetry, umbilicus, pulsations, and skin (Jarvis p. 542). Use this terminology on the documentation sheet for the abdomen section.
Significant finding that signals joint irritation; use contralateral side for comparison. Causes include effusion, synovial lining thickening, soft-tissue inflammation, or bony enlargement.
Break in a bone; a type of joint/bone deformity assessed during inspection.
Complete loss of contact between the two bones at a joint.
Bones stay in contact but alignment is off; a partial dislocation.
Muscle shortening that limits range of motion of a joint.
Stiffness or fixation of a joint; loss of normal movement.
Excess joint fluid causing swelling; a small amount is normal and not palpable, but palpable fluid is abnormal and shifts to cause visible bulging on another side of the sac.
Normally not palpable; when thickened it feels 'doughy' or 'boggy.' Warmth and tenderness signal inflammation.
Disease inside the joint capsule (e.g., arthritis) causing swelling and tenderness around the whole joint and limiting all planes of ROM in both active and passive motion.
Disease of a specific tendon, ligament, or nerve causing swelling and tenderness at one spot and affecting certain planes, especially active motion.
Client moves through voluntary range of motion; used first. Normal ranges of active and passive motion should be the same.
If limitation occurs with active ROM, examiner gently moves joint through passive motion with muscles relaxed; used to determine if limitation is mechanical or pain-related.
Extension beyond straight (e.g., chin lifted toward ceiling).

Person standing with gown open at back; spine is straight — imaginary vertical line runs from head through spinous processes and gluteal cleft; shoulders, scapulae, iliac crests, and gluteal folds are level; normal convex thoracic and concave lumbar curves from the side.
Age-specific screening test performed on infants during the musculoskeletal exam to screen for hip abnormalities.
Bowel sounds are declared absent only after 5 minutes of auscultation.
Normal aortic width by palpation is 2.5–4 cm.
Liver is considered enlarged if its edge is palpated more than 1–2 cm below the right costal margin.
A bruit is heard in 4%–20% of healthy people (usually under 40 years, celiac).
Medium intensity, duration, and pitch indicating solid organs, masses, fluid, adipose, or a distended bladder.

An imaginary vertical line runs from head through spinous processes and gluteal cleft; shoulders, scapulae, iliac crests, and gluteal folds are level with equal arm–thorax spaces. From the side there is normal convex thoracic and concave lumbar curve.
Spinous processes are straight and nontender; paravertebral muscles are firm with no tenderness or spasm.
Flexion 75–90° (lumbar concavity disappears, back forms a single convex C), hyperextension 30°, lateral bending 35°, and rotation 30° bilaterally; compared bilaterally and normally pain-free.
Dots placed on spinous processes while bending should form a straight vertical line on standing; a slight S-shape indicates a spinal curve.
Hold both hands back to back with wrists flexed 90° for 60 seconds; reproduction of numbness and burning is positive for carpal tunnel syndrome.
Direct percussion over the median nerve at the wrist; burning or tingling along the nerve distribution is positive for carpal tunnel syndrome.
Stroke the medial knee 2–3 times, tap the lateral side, and watch the medial hollow; a visible fluid wave indicates effusion of 4–8 mL and high risk for knee pain/progressive OA.
Compress the suprapatellar pouch and push the patella sharply against the femur; a tap heard as the patella bumps the femoral condyles indicates larger amounts of fluid present.
Supine; flex knee and hip, rotate the leg, apply valgus stress, and slowly extend; a 'click' felt or heard indicates a torn meniscus and warrants orthopedic referral.
Raise the extended leg just short of pain, then dorsiflex the foot, then raise the unaffected leg; reproduction or worsening of sciatic pain (worse with dorsiflexion) indicates herniated disc.
Supine; flex one knee to the chest while keeping the other leg straight; lifting of the opposite thigh off the table indicates a hip flexion deformity.
Infant hips are adducted then abducted/lifted; a clunk as the femoral head reseats is a positive test, done at every professional visit until age 1 year.
With knees flexed and compared side to side, one knee lower than the other is positive for hip dislocation.
Not described in the assigned Jarvis pages (pp. 585–613); Jarvis describes the Ortolani maneuver and the Allis test for hip dislocation instead.

True length is measured from anterior iliac spine to medial malleolus (normally equal or within 1 cm); apparent length from umbilicus to medial malleolus — unequal apparent lengths with equal true lengths occur with pelvic obliquity or hip adduction/flexion deformity.
Rules that govern imaging referral for knee and ankle injuries.
Rise from an armchair, walk 10 feet, turn, return, and sit; a healthy adult over 60 completes this in under 12 seconds, while 12 seconds or more indicates increased fall risk.
Do not attempt cervical motions if neck trauma is suspected.
Used when scoliosis is suspected in adolescents; a rib hump or unequal landmark elevation on forward bending suggests scoliosis.
Genu varum (>2.5 cm between knees with malleoli together) is normal for 1 year after walking begins; genu valgum (>2.5 cm between malleoli with knees together) is normal at 2–3½ years.
Flat foot is normal in infants and resolves by age 3; pronation is common 12–30 months, and pronation or lack of arch after age 3 is abnormal.

Flexion/extension = bending and straightening a limb at a joint; abduction/adduction = away from and toward the midline; pronation/supination = palm down and palm up; inversion/eversion = sole of foot inward and outward.
Abdominal assessment proceeds inspection, auscultation, percussion, then palpation (light before deep); light palpation is ~1 cm and deep palpation 5–8 cm.
The arc of movement of a joint, tested first as active (voluntary) ROM and then passive if limited; normally no tenderness, pain, or crepitation and equal bilaterally.
Inspection → auscultation → percussion → palpation; auscultate second because percussion/palpation can alter peristalsis.
Auscultate all four quadrants starting in the RLQ (ileocecal valve area) with the diaphragm.
Bowel sounds are called absent only after 5 minutes of continuous auscultation — a common test item.
Document bowel sounds as Present / Hyperactive / Hypoactive — that is the wording on her sheet.
Hyperactive = increased motility (early obstruction, gastroenteritis, diarrhea, laxatives, subsiding paralytic ileus); hypoactive/absent = surgery, peritonitis, paralytic ileus, complete obstruction.
Auscultate for bruits over aorta, renal, iliac, femoral arteries — that exact list.
Percussion is NOT recommended to determine liver span, splenomegaly, or bladder distention — but DO percuss the costovertebral angle for kidney tenderness.
Normal percussion = tympany predominates (air rises supine); dullness over solid organs, masses, fluid, adipose, distended bladder; hyperresonance = gaseous distention.

Light palpation ~1 cm and its purpose is an overall impression of skin surface and superficial musculature (not finding organs); deep palpation ~5–8 cm, with bimanual technique for very large/obese abdomens.
Assess tender areas LAST and watch nonverbal cues of discomfort.
If you feel an enlarged spleen, stop palpating — it is friable and can rupture.
Flexion = bending limb at joint; extension = straightening limb at joint.
Abduction = away from midline; adduction = toward midline.
Pronation = forearm turns palm down; supination = palm up.
Inversion = sole of foot inward (ankle); eversion = sole outward (ankle).
Client moves the part voluntarily (you model it); performed first, always. Ranges of active and passive motion should be the same.
You move the part with muscles relaxed; performed only if AROM shows limitation, comparing bilaterally.
Inspect then palpate (temperature, muscles, bony articulations, joint capsule); joints are normally non-tender.
